metadata.title: Merchant Services Residuals Explained | How Agents Get Paid Monthly
metadata.author: Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income
metadata.shortDescription:
**Nobody talks about this, but it’s why merchant services can create recurring income.**

How do merchant-services residuals actually work?

In this video, I break it down with a simple tire-shop example so you can understand the basic economics behind payment processing without getting buried in industry jargon.

At a high level, there are underlying costs associated with processing card transactions. The merchant is charged above those costs, creating a gross margin. Depending on your sales-rep compensation agreement, you may receive a percentage of that margin as residual income.

One merchant may only produce a relatively small amount.

But when you begin stacking 10, 50, 100, or more active merchants into a portfolio, those individual streams can begin adding up month after month.

That’s the power of the merchant-services business model:

**One merchant at a time.  
One transaction at a time.  
One portfolio built over time.**

🎓 **FREE Merchant Services Training — Merchant Service University:**  
https://merchantserviceuniversity.com

📘 **FREE eBook — The New Rules of Merchant Sales:**  
https://ebook.ezdirectsales.com

🎯 **Merchant Sales & Partnership Opportunities:**  
https://ezdirectsales.com

📚 **Merchant Sales Resources & Blogs:**  
https://iamjoewagner.com/merchant-sales-resources

💬 **All My Links:**  
https://link.me/iamjoewagner

The numbers used in this lesson are simplified hypothetical examples for educational purposes. Actual processing costs, margins, merchant profitability, residual splits, and earnings vary based on card mix, pricing, merchant activity, retention, and your compensation agreement.

CHAPTERS

00:00 How Merchant Services Residual Income Works  
00:19 The Tire Shop Profit Example  
00:42 How Payment Processing Creates Margin  
01:06 Cost + Markup = Gross Profit  
01:24 Simple $1,000 Transaction Example  
01:51 Where Your Merchant Residual Comes From  
02:14 Building a Portfolio of Merchant Accounts  
02:34 How Residual Income Can Compound  
02:56 One Merchant at a Time

a tire shop makes money selling tires, you can understand how residual income works in
merchant services. [music] Earlier we talked about interchange. For this lesson, think of interchange
as the underlying cost associated with processing the card. And like virtually every other business,
the opportunity for profit comes from the difference between the cost and what a
customer [music] is charged. So, imagine a tire shop buys a set of tires for $300. They sell
those tires to a customer for $350. How much did they make? It's simple. They made $50. They had
$300 in cost, they collected 350, the difference was $50. [music] That's their gross profit on the
tires. Merchant services works the exact same way. Every time a merchant accepts a card, there are
underlying costs associated with processing that transaction. Interchange is the majority part of
those costs. Now, interchange is not always the same. It can vary depending on the type of card,
how the card is accepted, whether it's swiped, [music] did they take it over the phone,
was it done on a website, and other factors. But, we're going to teach you all of that
elsewhere. [music] For now, let's not complicate this. Just remember, the basic concept is the same
as a tire shop. There's a cost, you sell it above that cost, and the difference equals your profit.
So, let's use some simple hypothetical numbers here. A merchant processes a $1,000 transaction.
For this simplified example, let's say the underlying interchange cost is 2% on that $1,000,
2% is $20. Now, let's say the merchant is charged by us 3%. That would be $30. So,
the merchant paid $30, our cost or the interchange was $20. [music] The difference is $10. That $10
represents the simplified gross margin that we're using for this example as a profit. And depending
on your compensation agreement, that profit is split between you and the ISO. And that's where
your residual income comes from. And this is where merchant services becomes really powerful. Don't
think about one $1,000 transaction, think about businesses processing transactions all day long.
And then again tomorrow, and then they do it again next week, and then next month, and next year.
Now, imagine you've signed 10 merchants. What about 50 merchants? 100 merchants? 500 merchants?
Potentially thousands [music] and thousands of transactions are creating small amounts of profit
throughout [music] your entire portfolio all day, all week, and all month long. And your share of
that profit is paid according to your sales rep agreement. [music] And as you continue adding
merchants, your residual portfolio continues to grow. So, don't overcomplicate residuals.
It's really that simple, just like a tire shop. There's a cost, we mark up that cost, and the
difference is what we keep, we split with the ISO on every single transaction multiplied by hundreds
and thousands and maybe even millions of dollars of processing and transactions. [music] For now,
understand the basic concept. Every merchant you add can potentially add another stream of
reoccurring monthly profit to your portfolio. One merchant at a time, one transaction at a time,
month after month. That's residual income in merchant services. [music]

metadata.shortDescription:
Want to learn merchant services and potentially build your own business in the payments industry?

🎓 GET FREE ACCESS TO MERCHANT SERVICE UNIVERSITY:
https://merchantserviceuniversity.com

Who actually makes the merchant services industry work — and where does the sales agent fit into all of it?

In this Merchant Service University lesson, I break down the major players behind every credit card transaction and explain their roles in plain English.

Think of the payments industry like a football team. Everyone has a position to play. You don't need to memorize every technical detail, but if you're going to build a business in merchant services, you should understand who the players are and how they work together.

YOU'LL LEARN:

• What issuing banks do
• What acquiring banks do
• The role of Visa, Mastercard, Discover and American Express
• How interchange, dues and assessments fit into processing
• What an Independent Sales Organization (ISO) is
• What an Independent Software Vendor (ISV) is
• How software and payments are becoming increasingly connected
• Where YOU fit as a merchant services sales agent

And that last part is important.

As the agent, you don't need to move money, build software, operate a bank, or understand every technical detail of payment processing.

Your role is to connect the pieces for the merchant.

You're the relationship builder.

You're the educator.

You're the problem solver.

You're the person helping business owners understand their options, improve their operations, and find payment and technology solutions that make sense for their business.

Behind every merchant account may be banks, card networks, processors, software providers and other partners — but someone still has to earn the merchant's trust and bring the relationship together.

That's where you come in.

Understanding the payments ecosystem gives you the confidence to stop feeling like someone who's simply "selling credit card processing" and start understanding your role as a trusted resource to the businesses you serve.

This video is part of my FREE Merchant Service University training series.

🎓 WANT THE FULL MERCHANT SERVICE UNIVERSITY EXPERIENCE?

Get FREE access here:
https://merchantserviceuniversity.com

Get educated. Learn the industry. Build your skills. Then decide where you want to take it.

MORE FREE MERCHANT SERVICES RESOURCES

📘 FREE EBOOK: NEW RULES OF MERCHANT SALES
The Future of Payments Is Changing & How to Stay Ahead of It

Download it FREE:
https://ebook.ezdirectsales.com

👉 MORE MERCHANT SALES RESOURCES:
https://iamjoewagner.com/merchant-sales-resources

💬 CONNECT WITH JOE WAGNER:
https://link.me/iamjoewagner

ABOUT JOE WAGNER

I'm Joe Wagner, founder of Merchant Service University. I've spent years in the merchant services industry personally selling accounts, building a residual portfolio, recruiting and training sales agents, and helping people better understand how to build a business in payments.

Merchant Service University was created to make that education accessible to people who want to learn the industry before deciding where and how they want to build their business.

Some of these parties include the issuing banks example Capital 1, the card networks, so Visa, Mastercard, AMX, Discover, the payment processing companies who actually process the payments. And then of course people like myself, which you know we go by various different names, merchant services agent, merchant services rep, there's independent sales organizations, and various other titles. And that's what makes this business so awesome. By bringing businesses into this ecosystem, we can actually earn residual income from those credit card transactions. It's almost like becoming a silent minority shareholder in multiple businesses. And once again, people, this is residual income, passive income. This isn't like clocking in at a job and and trading your time for money, right? That means instead of getting paid once, you can earn a small percentage every time a business processes payments. So, let's quickly go over the numbers. So, let's say you go out and sign up a cafe. The coffee shop owner's name is John. Let's assume that John's coffee shop will take about $20,000 per month in credit card sales. And let's also assume that the average processing rate is 2.80%. And look, I'm using 2.80% as an example, but between you and I, there are hundreds of different types of credit cards in circulation. And every single credit card in existence has a different cost associated to it. But once again, to keep this simple, we're going to say 2.80%. So, let's do the math, right? $20,000 per month in credit card sales times 2.80% means that at the end of the month, John will have $560 in transaction fees. Now, as mentioned earlier, multiple parties participate in this ecosystem. And the first party to actually take their share of that 560 bucks per month are the card brands. So, Visa, Mastercard, AMX, Discover. Let's assume that the cost of those cards was an average of 1.40% for example. So, if we do the math, $20,000 times 1.40% equates to $280 per month. that goes directly to the card brands, Visa and Mastercard. And so what we're left with is $280. That $280 per month is your gross profit. Now, typically this gross profit is now split between yourself in return for bringing this business into this ecosystem and your partner, which is either an ISO or a payment processor. Now, for those of you that are new to this world, an ISO or the payment processor is the company that gives you the ability to participate in this ecosystem. Now, typically the split will vary, but let's just assume that the split is 8020. So, 80% goes to you and 20% goes to your partner. So, 80% of 280 bucks is $224 per month in residual income. That means by bringing John into this ecosystem and by facilitating the ability for John to take credit card payments, you are now earning $224 per month for as long as John's in business. I truly want to emphasize that this is residual income. You did the work once and now every single month, $224 hits your bank account. That's $2,688 per year in passive income. That's $26,880 over the next 10 years. This is true predictable income. You can be on the beach hanging out with your family and you can guarantee that that $228 per month is hitting your bank account. But this is where the magic happens, right? Because it's all about compounding, right? Because listen, you know, $228 per month in residual income is not a whole lot of money. You know, it might cover a cell phone bill, but what if you had 10 clients? That's $2,240 per month in residual income for 10 clients. What about 50 clients? That's $11,200 per month in residual income. And now, what if you take a whole year or two and dedicate your time to this business? You go out and you sign up 100 clients. That's $22,400 per month in residual income. A lot of people can potentially semi-retire if they're earning $22,400 per month in residual income. And listen, the big idea is this. You're not chasing one-time commissions like a lot of the other business opportunities out there. You're stacking monthly cash flow client by client. And the magic is in the compound effect. Another reason why I personally have been in this industry myself for 15 years, which is crazy to think about, is the fact that it is 100% pandemic and recession proof. So, many of you may know that a short 6 years ago, we all went through this thing that starts with a co and ends with a vid. And it's crazy to think that so many local businesses around me were shutting their doors, right? And it was really sad to see. And I remember one night specifically looking at my residual report and one thing I noticed is that I was not taking a haircut. You see, a big reason why the merchant services industry is so powerful is directly tied to economic activity. Bottom line, businesses will always need to sell stuff. People will always need to buy things. And the most likely way that people buy things today is using plastic, right? They use a credit card and a debit card. So even if a business shut their doors during an economic crisis or a pandemic, for example, they're still taking payments online. And that's why this industry is so resilient. And look, in all fairness, there are a lot of other businesses out there that are solid, right? There's drop shipping, affiliate marketing, vending machines, ATM placement, insurance sales, starting a marketing agency. Like I've personally owned a healthy vending machine business myself. I had 14 healthy vending machines in multiple locations and I'll be frank with you, it was a nightmare of a business because ultimately you got to keep filling those vending machines up with inventory. The profit margins were so slim. The vending machines themselves were heavy. They needed to be transported. They also cost a lot of money. And you know, speaking about weight, it's the same thing with ATM placement. you know, ATM placement is actually quite close to merchant services, but ultimately it's the same issue, right? It's heavy. You got to transport it. It also costs a lot of money to buy an ATM. You have to constantly fill it up with cash or find somebody to fill it up with cash. Many times the business owners will want to take a profit share and some locations will absolutely suck. Affiliate marketing, drop shipping, you know, very, very small, thin profit margins. insurance sales. I love insurance, but you're dealing BTOC and not B2B. So, when you're selling business to consumer, ultimately what I noticed is that consumers, so if you're selling to regular people, they will always view a monthly payment as a burden versus when you're selling B2B like in merchant services. You see, selling to business owners is so much easier because business owners will view a monthly payment as the cost of doing business. And then of course there is the option of starting a brickandmortar traditional business right whatever that may be a restaurant for example and you know it goes without saying logically speaking that is a very very tough business to start you're talking sometimes you have to buy inventory it'll cost you hundreds of thousands of dollars to start you have to hire staff find the lease employee turnover and churn I'm getting a headache just thinking about it and sure you may think all right you know starting a traditional brick-and-mortar business is a tried and true battle tested business. And you're not wrong in thinking that. But let me tell you, the payment processing business has also been around for a very, very long time. This industry has gone through major shifts and phases. Believe it or not, in phase one, there was a time when business owners were not accepting credit cards. And people like myself would have to go convince these business owners that if they were to start accepting credit cards that they would actually get more customers. And that is phase one. In the beginning, the focus was simply helping businesses accept credit cards for the very first time. Many years later, we now enter into phase two of this industry, which is what I like to call the rate cutting war. In this phase, most businesses are now already accepting payments. And it's in this phase that competition absolutely exploded. As a matter of fact, it's in this phase that I personally started in this industry. And so people in this business would try to win over clients by simply saving business owners money on their credit card fees. So agent number one sets the business up at 2.80% and a few months later agent number two comes in and says, "Listen, Mr. Merchant, I can get you a rate of 2.4%. Ultimately saving you 40% on your overall monthly transaction fees." And listen, I get it. You know40 doesn't seem like a lot of savings, but if a business owner is taking even $50,000 per month in credit card transactions, that could be a few,000 a year in savings for that business. This ultimately created a race to the bottom because agent one is charging 2.80%, agent 2 is charging 2.40%. A third agent comes along and then offers, you know, 2% and so margins just kept getting squeezed. And so a few years later, this new program called cash discount or dual pricing made it legal and compliant for business owners to start passing on their fees to their customers. And so instead of saving40 on their overall monthly bill, now they're passing on all their fees over to their customers, essentially saving them even more because now instead of saving 40, you're saving, you know, a whole two to 3% on your overall transaction fees. And so we're going from a few hundred in savings to thousands of dollars in savings. But still, the value proposition revolved around savings. I've single-handedly seen multiple multiple people become multi-millionaires overnight because of this program, but all good things must come to an end. And at the time I'm recording this video, it has now been 10 years or so that these programs have become available. And so most business owners today either are already passing on their fees to customers or already know about the program and simply do not want to pass their fees on to their customers. And so there's no longer a novelty and uniqueness in this program. As mentioned, these programs still work when you're pitching merchants, but we are now coming to the end of phase three and entering into phase 4. Phase 4 is the SAS and technology era. You see, the modern payments business is no longer just about accepting payments. It's now about verticalization and specialty softwares. Let me give you an example, right? Softwares that are unique to specific industries. Example, a spa. So, an appointment booking software that gives a spa the ability to help their customers book into their calendar, provide reminders of appointments, and of course, integrate the payments right into the software. or even invoicing software that helps contractors send estimates, send invoices, and accept payments. There's literally so many different softwares, marketing automation platforms, loyalty programs, reputation management software, so on so forth. And it's funny because I always tell people these days what's happening essentially is software companies are basically payment companies in disguise. And it's not just about software, right? There's also modern payment technology and hardware. You see, even those POSOS systems that you see in retail stores or restaurants are also becoming much more sophisticated. Inventory management, seeding, employee management, and even some really cool products like selfch checkout systems and self-s serve kiosks. The days of the generalist are counted. The days of selling, savings, and support are also counted. When payment processing is combined with software and modern payment technology, the value proposition becomes much more powerful. You now have the ability to solve real pain points for many of these business owners in the form of software and technology and payment processing simply becomes the organic natural upsell. So, positioning is now better in the modern era. Let's quickly cover modern acquisition versus traditional acquisition. Basically, how do we get clients? Traditionally, merchant services was truly built around direct sales, door-nocking, you know, cold calling, networking, referral business, mailers, flyers, email campaigns, telemarketing, you name it. While these strategies still work and exist and I have nothing against cold calling and telemarketing as a matter of fact for years I built my payment business around telemarketing. But you see modern operators are now using the tools of today. I'm talking inbound marketing, content creation, digital lead generation, automated sales funnels, AI. And if you combine this new positioning of being the specialist and verticalization and pushing software and modern payment technology and you combine that with these much more modern marketing strategies, this now allows you to attract businesses and not have to chase them. And so this is what I mean by we're now entering this new gold rush because stacking residual income, if done correctly, has now become easier than ever. And listen, I said easier. I didn't say easy because nothing good is easy. So, in closing, the whole goal of this very first video of our 90day residual scaling sprint was simply to introduce you to the opportunity, but also explain how we're entering a new gold rush. In the next video, we're going to cover exactly how residual income really works and how to determine our magic number so that we can reverse engineer our goals. And so, thank you for making it to the end of this video. I will see you in the next one.

Visit us here: http://bestisoagent.com

Each year, hundreds of merchant services agents choose Shaw Merchant Group as the best merchant services company to work with. If you’re wondering why everyone gravitates towards this ISO agent program, then get ready to have all of your questions answered. Here are some of the greatest benefits of working with SMG’s ISO agent program.

Fast Start Bonus

We offer a performance-based fast start bonus that is payable for anyone that onboards more than the standard threshold of clients in the first 4 months. This program is designed to reward those experienced sales members that join our team and quickly learn how to sell this product. The bonus can reach up to $20,000, making it one of the most lucrative and competitive in the industry. 

14X Profit Based Bonus Structure

We will look at how much profit is generated on the account after they have been processing for one month and you earn 14 times of the total profit. Example: If we retain $100 in residuals in that month, the bonus would be 14 x $100 or $1,400. You would have already been paid $600, so we would pay you an additional $800 on that account. This bonus is capped at a max of $10,000 per merchant per location. With our Cash Discount Program it is easier than ever to earn huge bonuses with a 14x profitability bonus. This dual pricing model enables you to maximize your bonus at $10,000 on almost every merchant processing over $90k. 

Lifetime Passive Income

You will receive 50-70% of residual income based on the pay structure you select. You will share income on every available revenue stream. With SMG, You Get a True Interchange Revenue Split. Unlike other merchant iso programs, there is no basis points off the top for BIN sponsorship or for what they call hidden losses. Our sales partners earn more residual income with our 50/50 partner program than you would with our competition who claim to offer a higher percentage because their interchange cost (buy rate) is higher.

Free High-End Processing Equipment

Selling businesses on a new processing plan is much easier when you are able to effortlessly jump over the hurdle of the cost of the equipment. With this program, you can offer your clients free credit card terminals and free pos systems that they will need for their processing provider change. This lowers the barrier to switching and creates a higher conversion rate for you. 

Cash Discounting Program

When you are selling merchant services, one of the best assets of any partner program is more rewards and incentive programs that saves your merchant money. The cash discount program is one of the hottest new commodities in credit card processing, as it is designed to save the client thousands of dollars in credit card processing cost, instead passing on the fee to the consumer in a way that isn’t damaging to their own conversion rate and revenue. We offer this program to our clients and make it easy to understand and present for our sales partners. 

Multiple Processing Platforms

Even though we still use Global Payment and First Data as our processing platform, we have partnered with the EPX platform. EPX can optimize interchange, which means we can process the same transactions for less. This allows you to save merchants a ton of money and make more money yourself. 

Backoffice Tracking System

With our Sales Partner Portal (Dashboard) you can track your residuals all the way down to the transaction. You will have access to what your merchant paid for a specific transaction, how much the expense was and how much you were compensated. You're able to look at the merchant’s statement for comparison. With 100% transparency, you are now able to check whenever your want so you can be confident in building a profitable portfolio. 

Registered DBA Program

If you're serious about helping your merchants grow their businesses, we want to partner with you. Whether you're interested in becoming a Sales Partner, are already providing merchant services as a registered ISO, or you're a Sales Partner who wants to sell under your own name, SMG is the ISO partner you want. Our Registered DBA can get you up and running fast and save you thousands of dollars in card brand registration fees in the process.

Marketing Resources 

One of the things that Shaw Merchant Group is known for is providing our agents with the resources that they need to survive and thrive in a competitive business environment. This means marketing materials, frequent promotions, and other tools that help you to have more success and earn more commission!

Customer Support

SMG’s premium services don't just stop at the sale. Build the relationship with your merchants to new heights by providing them high-quality customer support to help them with any issue they are having with the merchant services they are provided.

If you’re brand new to merchant services and trying to figure out whether this industry is real, how it works, and if you can actually succeed in it — this video is for you.

Level 1, the curious new recruit, is the most misunderstood stage in the entire merchant services industry. After 15+ years in payments and working with thousands of reps, I can tell you this is where people either set themselves up for long-term success… or make mistakes that cost them years.

In this video, I break down Level 1 of the Five Levels of Merchant Service Mastery and walk through the exact stages required to move forward correctly.

You’ll learn:
• What merchant services actually is (without the hype)
• How payment processing works in plain English
• How reps get paid through residual income
• Why portfolio growth is the real asset in this business
• The mindset shift required to succeed as a 1099 entrepreneur
• Why overthinking keeps people stuck at Level 1
• How choosing the wrong ISO can destroy your future income

Merchant services isn’t complicated. Businesses accept credit cards. We help them set up the technology — terminals, POS systems, reporting tools — and we get paid for it. When done right, the business owner wins through better systems and support, and you build long-term residual income.

At Level 1, your job isn’t mastery.
Your job is understanding the basics, building confidence, and choosing the right ISO partner.

That decision matters more than most people realize.

metadata.title: Merchant Services ISO Agreements Explained | Vesting, Termination & Residual Rights
metadata.author: Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income
metadata.shortDescription:
A 100% residual split means nothing if your merchant-services agreement doesn’t protect your right to keep it.

Too many merchant sales agents compare ISO programs based on commissions and residual percentages first.

That’s backwards.

Your compensation plan tells you how much you can make.

Your agreement tells you whether you may be able to keep that income years from now.

In this video, I break down five things every merchant-services agent should understand before signing an ISO or agent agreement:

• Residual ownership and vesting
• Production requirements
• Termination provisions
• What happens if the ISO is sold or acquired
• Why the biggest residual split isn’t always the best opportunity

I learned this lesson the hard way.

Early in my merchant-services career, I spent roughly 3½ years building a portfolio and then lost the residual income because of language in an agreement I wasn’t educated enough to understand.

That experience changed how I evaluate partnerships today.

If you’re trying to build merchant services into a long-term income-producing portfolio, do not fall in love with the compensation plan before you read the contract.

Understand your residual rights.

Understand vesting.

Understand production requirements.

Understand termination.

And understand what happens if the company, management, or relationship changes.

That’s also why I believe:

Education first. Partnership second.

segments.text: If you're comparing merchant service companies based only on who offers the highest commission
and biggest residual split, you're looking at the wrong number first. Because a company can promise
you a 70% split, 80% split. Heck, they could even offer 100% residual split, but 100% of something
that you don't actually control and aren't protected on isn't the deal that you think it
is. So before you sign a single merchant account with any company, I'm going to show you the most
important things that I believe you should look for in your merchant sales agreement because your
compensation tells you how much that you make, but your agreement tells you whether you're going to
keep it for life or not. So number one is residual ownership investing. Start with the obvious. What
happens to your residuals? Are they vested? When do they vest? Do you continue receiving
them if you stop selling completely? If you don't sell a deal for 2 years, are they still going to
pay you? What happens if you leave the company? And what happens if the company terminates the
relationship or sells to another company? Don't accept. Don't worry about it. We always take care
of our agents. That sounds great. Now, show me where it's in writing. If you're going to spend
years building a portfolio, the agreement should clearly explain what happens to that income under
all these circumstances. Number two is look for production requirements. This is something agents
can easily overlook. Does your residual depend on continuing to produce? If it does, that's
not lifetime residual income that you can walk away from and keep collecting. That's a job. So,
are there minimums or annual requirements? Can your split change if production drops? Can your
residual rights change if you stop actively selling? Maybe you're crushing it today, but
what happens 5 years from now? What happens if you want to retire? The whole point of residual income
is to control your time freedom. And you may want to enjoy it. And last thing you need is somebody
telling you you're not going to get your residuals because you didn't produce a deal for the last 90
days. The whole reason many of us build residual income is to eventually have the freedom to not
work. So make sure your agreement doesn't require you to keep running forever just to protect what
you've already built. Number three is understand termination. This is a big one. Read the
termination provisions. Under what circumstances can the company terminate your agreement? And more
importantly, what happens to your portfolio if they do? There is a massive difference
between terminating your ability to submit new applications and terminating the residual
income you've spent years building. Know the difference. Understand the language. And if you

card processing fees and how customers

We'll break down what dual pricing is, its pros and cons, and everything
you need to consider before implementing it with your business.
Dual pricing
is becoming a popular way for merchants to avoid credit card processing fees
by offering different prices based on the customer's payment method.
But what exactly does dual pricing mean, and how does it compare
to other pricing strategies like cash discount or surcharging?
Let's break it down.
Dual pricing
refers to a system where merchants display two different prices,
one for cash payments and another for credit card payments.
The customer has the option to pay the cash price,
the original price of the product, or they can choose
the credit card price, which includes the cost of processing.
You don't have to change your pricing or inventory in any way.
When you set up this payment model with the processor,
your merchant account is configured for dual pricing.
For example, when going to a cafe, you may see a sign saying something
like Bacon Cheeseburger for a cash price of $17.66
and a bacon cheeseburger for a credit card price of $18.37.
The fee here will be about 4.02% if the customer is paying at the counter.
The POS screen will show the cash price and the card price
if the customer is paying at the end of the meal.
The receipt will list the two prices at the bottom.
The price when paying with cash, which again is a $17.66,
and the cash price paid with a card, which is the $18.37.
One common question is the difference between dual pricing and a cash discount.
While both strategies offer a lower price for cash payments than card payments,
a cash discount works by offering a discount from the regular price
when the customer pays with cash.
In contrast, dual pricing as two separate prices the cash price
and the card price, with the cash price being the initial sticker price.
Another point of confusion is dual pricing versus Surcharging.
With Surcharging, merchants charge
an additional fee for customers who choose to pay with a credit card.
On the other hand, dual pricing provides a transparent option where
both prices, cash and credit are displayed from the start,
giving customers a choice without any surprise fees at checkout.
Surcharging also has many regulations and state
rules to follow, whereas dual pricing does not.
If you want to learn more about Surcharging,
check out our video on it here or linked in the description.
The advantages of
dual pricing are number one lower processing costs.
Dual pricing allows businesses to pass credit card or debit card
processing fees to customers paying with cards, preserving profit margin.
This flexibility helps you cover
transaction fees while giving customers payment options.
Number two transparent by displaying both cash and card prices upfront.
Customers know exactly what they'll pay based on their chosen method.
This clarity can build trust and reduce any surprises at checkout.
Number three, it encourages cash payments.
Offering a lower cash price
can motivate customers to pay with cash, helping you avoid processing fees.
And lastly, number four compliance.
Unlike Surcharging, dual pricing is generally more accepted
and legally compliant, giving you peace of mind with fewer legal concerns.
On the other hand, the disadvantages of dual pricing are.
Number one customer confusion.
Some customers may not be familiar with dual pricing,
potentially leading to confusion with the higher credit card price.
If the price gap between cash and card is too large, it could discourage sales,
particularly if customers perceive the credit card price as unfair.
It's important to strike a balance between offering a cash incentive
and keeping the credit card price reasonable.
Number two more work for staff.
If you incorporate dual pricing, you may be adding more work for you or your staff.
As mentioned, customers may be confused by the difference between the list price
and the increased credit card price they pay.
You and your staff
may have to spend a little extra time explaining this discrepancy
and getting your customers to understand why you're using this pricing strategy.
Number three compliance issues.
Implementing dual pricing requires setup with a processor
that supports the system, along with ensuring compliance with the law.
And with the payment card Industry data Security standard.
And number four, these may still apply even with dual pricing.
Some payment processors may charge small transaction or service fees.
So review all costs to ensure this model truly benefits your business.
Before implementing dual pricing in your business.
There are a few factors to consider.
First, think about how your customers will react to seeing two different prices.
Customer communication is key to making dual pricing successful.
Second, you'll want to work

Choosing the right provider

How the Dual Pricing Cash Discount Works

The process is simple. Just let us know you want to be a part of the Cash Discount Program. We’ll provide you with signage that states the percentage credit card customers will pay if they pay with a credit card.

You go about business as normal, processing payments as you normally do. If you have a credit card paying customer, our terminal will calculate the cost for you. There’s no extra work on your part, and you reward the cash-paying customers with a discount – it’s that easy.

The Cash Discount Program is Great for Business

You may think the cash discount program would turn off your credit card paying customers, but it won’t. A majority of customers don’t mind paying a slightly higher price, (cents on the dollar really) for the convenience of carrying credit cards versus cash.

You and the customers come out the winner in the deal. You show honesty and integrity by providing signage that lets customers know of the price difference if they use a credit card and you reward those that choose to pay cash. Eventually, more customers will catch on and have cash available when they shop at your store - after all, who doesn't love a little discount, right? Take a look below at the summery of benefits:

Lower Processing Fees

The main benefit of a cash discount program is that it results in lower or zero processing fees. While many don’t give a second thought to what the processing fees are on any given transaction, business owners certainly know that these fees do add up and can affect margin in a very real way. When merchants use Edge pricing they are, in effect passing on that processing fee to the customer. Over time, this can save merchants thousands and provide them with a higher margin on their sales.

Discounts for Customers

What customer doesn’t love a discount? Being able to provide every customer that pays in cash with a discount is not only a very marketable promotion, but it helps to make your customers happy. Customers love going to businesses that offer a cash discount because it allows them to feel as if they are getting a good deal and somewhat have control over what they pay at your establishment. When it comes to happy customers, it is very hard to put a price tag on that.

Increased Loyalty/Happiness

When your customers are continuously having positive experiences at your business and are getting to know your establishment as a place that offers a cash discount, that can only help you. This creates loyalty and happiness in your customer base and helps to establish brand and customer loyalty. This is a very valuable asset and it can help to offer consistent cash discounts to your customers.

Easy to Deploy

In truth, it is growing increasingly easy to deploy a cash discount program and with all of the resources that we provide to our merchants, it is easier than ever.

With our cash discount program POS, you will be able to process a wide variety of payments from all major credit card providers. This offers your customers even more convenience and helps to build loyalty time and time again.

Free POS Equipment

Don’t worry about the cost of upgrading to a whole new system--we have you covered. We provide free POS equipment to our merchants to once again make working with the Edge program as easy as possible. When you work with us, there will be very little to be worried about.

Fast Funding

We are known for providing fast funding to our merchants. It’s hard to operate a business when your cash flow is being restricted, and that is why we put a focus on making payments accurate, concise, and fast to provide you with a business partner that you can trust to keep your financial interests at the forefront.

Flexible Contracts

Worried about getting locked into a long contract? Don’t be. We don’t believe in limiting the options of our merchants and that is why we offer flexible contract options that don’t lock you in for years at a time. With the Edge cash discount program, you’ll have options, which are extremely valuable to have when operating a business. You can pivot at a moment’s notice, should you need to.

Easy to Understand

From a customer and merchant perspective, operating on a new POS system can be complicated and difficult. That isn’t the case with Edge. We have structured this program to make it as easy as possible to understand and use so that any business can use this program to their advantage.

metadata.title: Dual Pricing Done Right: 2026 Practical Guide To Cash Discount And Surcharging Compliance | PEP106
metadata.author: Global Legal Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Surcharging caps. Debit card limits. Fines that flow through banks. If you’ve ever wondered who really profits from card payments, this conversation will change how you see things.

Checkout is turning into a trust test. Customers hate surprise fees, merchants hate absorbing card costs, and the rules around surcharging, cash discount, and dual pricing keep getting more confusing. We sit down with Clark Krimer from National ePayment (https://nationalepayment.com/) to get practical about what actually works at the point of sale and why so many business owners only change pricing once the shop next door does it.

We break down why merchants hesitate to adopt dual pricing and what actually happens when customers see a cash price next to a card price. Clark Krimer explains how payments sales works in the real world and why better pricing disclosure is the missing piece in credit card processing.

• merchants waiting for nearby businesses to adopt dual pricing first
• why customers assume surcharges are merchant profit
• how dual pricing differs from surcharging and cash discounting
• Visa-style disclosure expectations and the operational challenge of changing prices
• Do Price Digital Labeler printing cash and card prices
• California restaurant fee disclosures and why menus create risk
• how fines and enforcement pressure flow through banks and processors
• why payments education stays low and transparency stays hard

We talk through the real economics of credit card processing fees: why a simple surcharge cap often fails to cover the full spread, why debit card restrictions complicate “pass-through” pricing, and why customers often assume the merchant is pocketing the difference. From there, we dig into the compliance problem that trips up otherwise honest businesses. If a fee is disclosed poorly, especially in restaurants and other high-traffic environments, it can trigger complaints, fines, or even litigation. The conversation also touches California’s junk fee environment and why menu disclosure is becoming a legal flashpoint.

Then we get hands-on with a surprisingly effective fix: Do Price Digital Labeler, a tool designed to make dual pricing easy in retail by printing a single label with both the cash price and the card price. It’s a small operational detail with a big impact on price transparency, customer clarity, and brand rules alignment.

If you care about payments compliance, merchant services strategy, or the future of surcharging and dual pricing, this one is for you. Subscribe, share this with a merchant who is struggling with fees, and leave a review with your take: should the customer see two prices everywhere?

**Matters discussed are all opinions and do not constitute legal advice.  All events or likeness to real people and events is a coincidence.**

metadata.title: What is Dual Pricing? | Payment Insights
metadata.author: CCSalesPro
metadata.shortDescription:
Dual Pricing can vary from statement to statement. There are a few signs that the statement you are looking at is a dual pricing processing statement.

One of the first ways to tell is that the statement will have a flat rate above 3%. This number looks like a flat rate, but it is typically going to be higher than a traditional flat rate.

The second way to determine if it is a dual pricing statement is somewhere on the statement it will have a line item on the statement showing a credit. This will either be one individual line item that shows the entire amount as a credit, or it would be listed as a daily discount showing that percentage collected on each day.

Some companies have minimal statement information to keep their pricing structure hidden from competitors. Instead of showing the total fees the merchant was paying, some statements only show smaller fees and exclude the entire discount fees.

If you run a restaurant, retail store, service business, auto shop, salon, or any business that accepts card payments, this video will help you understand how to reduce the impact of processing fees while staying informed about the rules.

metadata.title: The Future of Merchant Services: 7 Things Every Payments Sales Agent Must Understand
metadata.author: Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income
metadata.shortDescription:
The merchant services industry is changing fast.

If you're still selling payment processing based primarily on rates, fees, and credit card terminals, you're already falling behind.

Business owners today are looking for much more. They want technology that helps them operate more efficiently, automate repetitive work, understand their customers, improve cash flow, and ultimately grow their business.

In this video, I break down what I call the Modern Commerce System and the 7 pillars every merchant services sales agent should understand if they want to build a long-term career in the payments industry.

After more than 16 years in merchant services, I believe the future belongs to sales professionals who evolve from simply being "payment processing reps" into trusted business technology advisors.

You'll learn about:

1. Faster Access to Cash
Why faster funding, banking relationships, and working capital are becoming increasingly important to business owners.

2. Modern Business Technology
How POS systems, inventory management, scheduling, online ordering, payroll, reporting, and integrated business software are changing merchant services.

3. Customer Growth
Why customer data, loyalty programs, automated marketing, and repeat business should become part of the conversation.

4. AI & Automation
How artificial intelligence is helping businesses analyze data, automate repetitive work, create marketing campaigns, and make faster decisions.

5. Connected Commerce
Why businesses need to accept payments and interact with customers in-store, online, through invoices, appointments, subscriptions, mobile environments, and other channels.

6. Business Intelligence & Data
Every transaction creates valuable information. Modern businesses need systems that turn that information into insights they can actually use.

7. The Right Merchant Services Partnership
Technology alone isn't enough. Training, implementation, merchant support, ongoing education, fair agreements, and strong partnerships can determine whether you build a portfolio that lasts.

The biggest shift is simple:

Stop thinking like a payment processing salesperson and start thinking like a business advisor.

Your job isn't to force every merchant into the exact same platform.

Your job is to understand the business, identify its problems, and help the owner build the right technology stack for how that business actually operates.

That's where I believe the future of merchant services is headed.

🎓 WANT TO BUILD A CAREER IN MERCHANT SERVICES?

I created Merchant Service University to teach aspiring and existing payments professionals the fundamentals of:

• Merchant services
• Payment processing
• Modern commerce technology
• POS systems
• Residual income
• Portfolio building
• Merchant services contracts
• Technology partnerships
• Evaluating ISOs and payment companies
• Building a long-term merchant services business

I'm currently giving qualified people who want to potentially partner with me access to Merchant Service University.

Complete the certification, learn the industry, and then let's have a conversation about your goals and whether one of the companies and partnerships in my network could be the right fit for you.

👉 Get Started:
https://ezdirectsales.com

🎓 Merchant Service University:
https://merchantserviceuniversity.com

📘 Merchant Sales Resources:
https://iamjoewagner.com/merchant-sales-resources

🔗 Connect With Joe Wagner:
https://link.me/iamjoewagner

Subscribe for more videos about merchant services, payment processing, POS technology, AI in payments, merchant sales, residual income, FinTech, and building a payments business.

segments.text: Hi, my name is James Shepherd.
In this video, I’m going to be talking to you about cash discounting residuals – the
most important variable.
There is one area where I think cash discounting has really kind of confused a lot of merchant
services reps, that are used to doing interchange plus pricing.
That is understanding the effect of the average ticket size on cash discounting.
I think the first thing we have to do is we have to reclassify cash discounting for the
purposes of this conversation as flat rate pricing.
Because that is really what it is.
As far as, you know, you don’t really care about the discount they are giving when you
pay cash.
What you care about is the service fee that is collected when they don’t.
Really all you are doing is you are pricing merchants on flat rate pricing.
I mean that is really what it comes down to, right?
It’s flat rate pricing.
Flat rate pricing is very different from interchange plus pricing.
It can be a lot more profitable, but it can also be less profitable.
You have to understand how this works.
When you are doing interchange plus pricing for instance, what you are doing is you are
passing the cost of interchange and the bank fees and the dues and assessments and all
that through to the merchant.
Then you are adding on a 50 basis points of mark-up or whatever, so your profit is always
the same.
Whether it’s a $5 transaction or it’s a $30 transaction, or it is $1,000 transaction,
it doesn’t matter.
Your profit as a percentage of volume is always the same, but here is where you run into problems.
When you switch over to flat rate pricing, there is an interesting thing that happens.
With flat rate pricing, there is a sweet spot.
It is usually between $25 to $70 average ticket size.
So if you have a merchant that has an average ticket size of $27, $59, $43, in that kind
of sweet spot range, then usually that’s where your costs are going to be lowest.
The reason is really simple.
The reason is because a lot of people are using check cards, signature debit, and those
signature debit cards have a regulated interchange cost.
That regulated interchange cost is all about the per item fee.
It’s 22 cents plus 5 basis points.
So a 22 cent kind of fixed cost plus your processor fees and whatever else you are at
30, 32 cents.
So that 30 to 32 cents is really kind of meaningless on a transaction that is even $30.
That’s only like 1%.
It is very low interchange cost.
So if you are pricing somebody at collecting a service fee of 3%, you probably have a good
180 basis points of mark-up or so.
That’s a pretty big deal, right?
You are making a lot of money.
But the thing you need to understand is that there are two edges.
Whenever you have a problem, you always got to think about the edges.
The two edges are what about the really low average ticket size merchant.
If somebody has an average ticket size of $10, well now all of a sudden that 32 cents
becomes 3.2%.
That’s a really big problem because if your service fee is 3%, but the cost of servicing
that transaction is 3.2%, your residuals are negative 20 basis points.
You are losing money.
You have to understand that if you are doing flat rate pricing and you are getting below
that $25 average ticket range, you have to understand that your profits get lower and
lower and lower with the size of the transaction.
A $5 transaction that has a 32 cent cost, that’s 6.4% cost.
So if you are collecting 4%, 3.99%, you are still way under water with that deal.
On the lower ones, you’ve got to be thinking about do I want to use a per item fee, or
do I want to make sure I’m matching out the percentage and going to get to 3.99%,
getting it as high as I can and thinking through which strategy you want to use because you
may want instead of doing a 3.99% kind of flat rate service fee pricing, you may instead
want to do 59 cents a transaction, or something like that when they are really low, but you’ve
got to think through it.
You’ve got to look at these average ticket and really draw it out and see what it’s
going to be.
Okay.
That’s first of all.
The other edge is actually the larger one too.
One thing that will surprise you is if you have a merchant that does say an average of
$150 transaction or so, many times a business like that, maybe it is a jewelry store or
something along those lines.
They are taking a ton of reward cards, corporate reward cards.
Some of you are doing cash discounting on B to B businesses and things like that.
You are not thinking about the implications.
There are a lot of cards out there.
These corporate reward cards that have a 2.5% interchange cost.
If you have a 2.5% interchange cost, what’s going to happen is you are going to have a
huge cost and if you are only charging them a 3% service fee or whatever, you are not
going to make any money.
You need to understand what’s the average ticket size of the merchant and also what
is the mix of cards that they are taking and make sure that you understand if you are doing
really low ticket, you want to make sure you are doing a per item.
If you are doing really high ticket, you probably want to get your percentage up a little bit,
so it covers those corporate rewards and other rewards cards that are going to have a higher
cost.
My name is James Shepherd.
Hopefully this video will help you to maximize your cash discounting residuals.

metadata.title: Traditional Credit Card Pricing vs. Dual Pricing: Which One to Choose For Your Business
metadata.author: O3 Merchant Services
metadata.shortDescription:
In today's video, I will break down the differences between traditional credit card pricing and dual pricing and assist businesses to seriously consider the dual pricing structure to save money. Enjoy watching this video! Comment below and subscribe to our channel for more industry-specific videos related to credit card processing.

✅Read the full Blog: ​https://o3merchant.com/blogs/ 

O3 Merchant has been a trusted Merchant Service Provider in Los Angeles for over 25 years, providing safe, secure, easy payment solutions to small business owners.

To get more information regarding O3 Merchant Services: support@o3merchant.com (818) 500-0001

#creditcardprocessing
#dualpricing 
#cashdiscount

metadata.title: How to Lower Credit Card Processing Fees for Small Businesses - GoDaddy
metadata.author: GoDaddy
metadata.shortDescription:
How can small businesses lower credit card processing fees? This practical guide explains interchange, assessment, processor, and chargeback fees; flat-rate versus interchange-plus pricing; fixed per-transaction fees; and how to calculate your effective processing rate. Your effective rate is total processing costs divided by total card sales. 

👉 Explore point-of-sale and payment options for your business: 
https://www.godaddy.com/payments/point-of-sale 

👉 Read the related guide: How to cut credit card processing fees, 9 things you can do:
https://www.godaddy.com/resources/skills/lower-credit-card-fees 

⏱️ CHAPTERS 
00:00 How can you lower credit card processing fees? 
00:10 What are credit card processing fees? 
00:41 What's the difference between flat-rate and interchange-plus pricing? 
01:15 What fixed fees affect your effective rate? 
01:46 What should you check before switching payment processors? 
02:09 What card-minimum and credit-card pricing rules apply? 
02:30 How can payment settings and fraud prevention help? 
03:01 How do you review payment processing statements? 
03:22 What are GoDaddy's in-person payment processing rates? 
03:53 Who is eligible for Rate Saver? 

Built for U.S. businesses that accept in-person payments, this video also covers what to review before switching payment processors: total cost, card-minimum rules, payment gateway settings, fraud prevention, and statement review. Flat-rate pricing uses a published price per sale, while interchange-plus pricing combines card-dependent costs with a processor markup. 

For eligible in-person businesses, GoDaddy offers flat-rate processing that starts at 2.5% + 0¢ per transaction, or 2.3% + 0¢ with a Point of Sale Plus plan.* Eligible businesses with a Point of Sale Plus plan can also turn on Rate Saver and pay as low as 0% on eligible credit card processing, with eligible in-person debit at 1.9% + 0¢.* 
 
Illustrative processing-fee scenario: A business processing $10,000 a month across 1,000 in-person transactions would incur $230 a month in processing fees at GoDaddy's Point of Sale Plus rate of 2.3% + 0¢. An illustrative comparison rate of 2.6% + 15¢ on the same volume would produce $410 a month in processing fees. With Rate Saver active on an assumed 50/50 split of eligible credit and eligible debit volume, the estimated processing fee is $95 a month: as low as 0% on eligible credit and 1.9% + 0¢ on eligible debit. That is a $135 monthly reduction versus Point of Sale Plus processing without Rate Saver and a $315 monthly difference versus the illustrative comparison rate.* 

*Processing-fee example assumes $5,000 eligible credit and $5,000 eligible debit in-person volume; excludes subscriptions, hardware, and other fees; and is illustrative only. Point of Sale Plus requires a subscription. Rate Saver is not available in all U.S. states or for ecommerce transactions. Actual rates may vary. segments.text: Cash price, ten dollars. Card price, ten dollars and thirty-five cents.
Is that legal? It depends entirely on how you do it.
Here's dual pricing, cash discounts, and zero-fee processing, explained.
First, zero-fee processing is not free processing.
Interchange and card network fees are still paid on every card sale.
The cost doesn't disappear. It mostly moves from you to your customer.
There are three ways to do that.
A surcharge: you post your normal price, and add a fee at checkout for credit cards.
A cash discount: you post the card price, and take money off for cash.
Dual pricing: both prices are shown everywhere, and the customer picks.
The price you post decides which rules apply.
Surcharging carries the strictest rules.
Credit cards only, never debit.
Under Visa's rules, it's capped at your cost of acceptance, and never above three percent.
You give thirty days' advance notice, post signs at the door and till, and itemize the fee on the receipt.
Cash discounts and dual pricing have fewer rules, but they must be real.
Signs at the entrance and the till explain that two prices apply.
For dual pricing, every price exists twice: shelf labels, menus, your website, even quotes.
Your POS stores two real prices, not a percentage added at the till.
And the receipt shows which price the customer paid.
Here's where programs go wrong.
Only some prices get updated.
The difference is a round number, like four percent, instead of your actual cost.
Nobody told the staff.
And if you post the cash price and add a card fee at the till, it's a surcharge, whatever it's called.
So who does dual pricing suit?
Businesses with a manageable number of prices, a capable POS, and customers who still pay cash.
It's a poor fit for large or fast-changing catalogs, or where almost nobody pays cash.
And state rules vary and change often. Check yours, ask your processor, and get legal advice if the sums are large.
Before choosing any of these, know your effective rate.
That's your total card fees, divided by your card sales.
If it's lower than you think, passing the cost on may not be worth it at all.
Dual pricing works when both prices are real. The full guide is linked below.

segments.text: Can you legally add three percent when a customer pays by card?
Sometimes. It depends on the card, your state, and your setup.
Here are the rules, and what the Visa and Mastercard settlement would change.
A surcharge adds a fee on top of your normal price, for credit cards.
A cash discount posts one price, and takes money off for cash.
Dual pricing shows a cash price and a card price, side by side.
Your signs and receipts decide which one you're really running, not what you call it.
If you surcharge, the card network rules are strict. Under Visa's rules:
Credit cards only. Debit and prepaid cards can't be surcharged, even debit run as credit.
The fee can't be more than your cost of accepting that card, and never more than three percent.
Give your acquirer thirty days notice before you start.
Put a sign at the door, and another at the till.
And show the surcharge as its own line on the receipt.
Other card brands have similar, but not identical, rules. Meet the strictest.
State law is separate. Visa's guidance lists Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts and Oklahoma among the states that prohibit or limit surcharging.
These laws change often, so check your state's current rules with your processor or an attorney.
So why surcharge at all? Rewards cards.
Card issuers pay for points mostly through interchange, the fee you pay on every card sale.
On an eighty dollar sale, that's about one dollar forty on a standard credit card, but about two dollars on premium rewards.
And today, if you accept a brand's credit cards, you generally must accept all of them.
In June twenty twenty-six, a federal judge gave a revised Visa and Mastercard settlement preliminary approval.
Final approval is still pending, and a convenience store trade group has said it will appeal if the deal is approved.
Even if approved, changes likely won't reach merchants until twenty twenty-seven, and an appeal could delay them further.
If it's approved, here's what would change.
Merchants could decline some premium rewards and commercial cards.
Credit surcharges would be capped at your cost, or three percent, whichever is lower.
Average credit interchange would drop by about a tenth of a point, for five years.
And standard consumer credit interchange would be capped at one point two five percent, for eight years.
It wouldn't cover debit or American Express, and state laws would still apply.
Before you add any card fee, run this checklist.
Know your real cost first: your effective rate, total fees divided by card sales.
Check your state's law.
Make sure your terminal can surcharge credit only, and itemize it.
Or skip the fee: a cash discount, or a lower processing markup, may be the simpler fix.
Rules vary by state, and this isn't legal advice.

segments.text: ﻿Welcome back, Mavericks!
Thanks for tuning in today as we tackle the not-so-fun subject of credit card surcharging.
While it may not be the most glamorous topic,
understanding credit card fees is essential to owning and operating a small business.
So, we’re going to break down what surcharges are and whether or not
it is a good idea to add a credit card surcharge policy yourself.
Let’s start by defining our terms.
A surcharge is a fee that some businesses tack on to a credit
card transaction to cover the cost of what the credit card processor charges.
Essentially, it’s a way for businesses to pass the
cost of transaction fees onto the customer instead of absorbing them.
Some businesses may also offer cash discounting,
which offers customers a slightly lower price if they pay with cash or a debit card.
An important thing to keep in mind is that the practice of surcharging
is not legal everywhere in the United States.
Currently, you are not allowed to add a surcharge if you operate in Connecticut,
Massachusetts, or the territory of Puerto Rico.
In the states of California, Florida, Kansas, Maine, New York, Oklahoma, Texas, and Utah,
anti-surcharging laws exist but are currently unenforceable due to recent court decisions.
If your company operates in multiple states,
you can add surcharges in the states where that practice is legal.
However, the practice of incentivizing customers to pay with cash by offering
discounted prices is legal in all 50 states and US territories.
Now, let’s take a quick look at how some of the most popular credit cards handle
the practice of surcharging, as each one has slightly different guidelines.
If you’re thinking about implementing a surcharge,
the first thing you’ll need to do is notify the card association and
merchant services provider of your intent in writing at least 30 days in advance.
Note that this policy does not apply to American Express unless you comply with all other rules.
The amount that you can tack on to a surcharge is not allowed to be greater than the fee of
the credit card transaction and is capped at 4% (and 2% if you’re operating in Colorado).
This ensures that businesses can not profit from adding a surcharge.
You are also required to place a notice of your surcharge policy at
the entrance of your business and near the point of sale.
For online businesses, you must post a notice on your checkout page.
The surcharge amount must also be listed on the receipt as a separate line item.
(Again, this policy does not apply to American Express transactions.)
For Visa and Mastercard, you can apply brand-level or product-level surcharges,
meaning you can apply the same surcharge across all Visa or Mastercard purchases
or on a particular product, but you can not apply both types of surcharge.
Once you understand these guidelines and have sent your notice, you’ll need to make sure
that your payment gateway is programmed to accurately record the surcharges.
Now that you understand the requirements for adding surcharges on transactions,
let’s get to the big question: Should your small business consider adding a surcharge?
This isn’t an easy question, but more businesses have been
adopting this policy as costs have increased and margins have tightened.
It has also become easy in most states to implement.
You will definitely run the risk of alienating some of your customers,
particularly if you’re competing with big box stores.
In the current economy, customers are always looking for deals and ways to cut costs.
However, if you are a unique local business and have a supportive customer base, you may
have more luck garnering support for the small fee that could help your business’s bottom line.
If you do find that your processing fees are prohibitively high,
you might want to search for a different provider.
If you don’t have one already, we would encourage you to look at an interchange-plus pricing option,
which is generally more affordable and has transparent pricing options.
Don’t know what interchange-plus is?
We’ll include a link to an article explaining that pricing model in our description.
So that’s going to do it for us today Mavericks!
Thanks again for watching, and make sure to hit the thumbs up button if you enjoyed this video.
Also, subscribe to our channel to make sure you
don’t miss any other helpful content for small businesses.
We’ll see you next time!

metadata.title: Ban on debit and credit card surcharges | The Business | ABC NEWS
metadata.author: ABC News (Australia)
metadata.shortDescription:
The Reserve Bank of Australia has introduced reforms that will remove surcharges on debit, prepaid and credit cards on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa.  The ban is expected to save consumers about $1.6 billion in surcharge fees each year, with businesses saving $200 million in surcharge fees annually.  The package of reforms also includes lowering the caps on interchange fees paid by Australian businesses, with a focus on small businesses, which currently pay the highest fees.  Caps on interchange fees for foreign card payments will also be introduced.  The RBA expects these reforms to save businesses $910 million each year.  But the changes could cost the banks around $660 million a year and put reward points in the firing line.   Simon Birmingham from the Australian Banking Association says the Reserve Bank even thinks "banks could look at higher fees or charges on credit cards, interest rates and other changes to those credit cards." "In the UK, we saw things like annual fees and interest rates go up. Access to credit, we think, could be an issue as a result on this, as banks need to think about the profitability of their credit card businesses, " said Visa Oceania group country manager Alan Machet.  Visa and Mastercard both welcome the surcharge ban.  Mr Machet said the Reserve bank has more work to do and warned payments could move to other unregulated networks, pushing the overall costs in the system up.  

A key part of this change is to give consumers a fairer go at the shops.  But even the RBA expects the 16 per cent of businesses that surcharge may now increase their prices to cover transaction costs, pushing inflation even higher.  Andrew McKellar from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said "these costs are still going to be worn somewhere in the system ... so small businesses are either going to absorb that cost or they're going to have to pass it on their customers."

The final part of the reforms is to increase transparency and competition over fees, with eftpos, Mastercard, Visa and the big acquirers like NAB, Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and ANZ to publish the fees they charge to businesses.  Most of the reforms are due to take effect from October 2026.

metadata.title: ‘Unintended consequences’: Labor’s credit card surcharge ban sparks backlash
metadata.author: News24
metadata.shortDescription:
Backlash is mounting over the unintended consequences of Labor's ban on credit card surcharges.

Renters are the latest to be caught up as businesses demand a rethink.

Restaurants and cafés say the ban has forced them to raise their prices.

segments.text: Backlash is mounting over the unintended
consequences of Labor's ban on credit
card surcharges. Renters are the latest
to be caught up as businesses demand a
rethink.
>> It's the central promise of Labor's ban
on credit card surcharges.
>> The price you see is the price you pay.
>> But the prices they see are going up as
business owners flood social media to
say they have no choice but to pass on
the cost of covering processing fees.
>> Small to medium operators, we have no
choice. We're sort of held by the
throat.
>> The unintended consequences of Labor's
call are mounting. Last week, the tax
office announced that rather than absorb
the cost itself, it would instead refuse
all credit card payments from November
>> We can't expect SMEs, particularly in
the building sector, to keep taking
these hits.
>> The Prime Minister must reverse this
decision immediately.
>> News 24 has made multiple requests for
an interview with the tax commissioner
to explain this decision, all of which
so far have been declined. Instead, Rob
Heffernan pleading his case in a lengthy
statement released late on Friday night.
He argues it would not be tenable for
the ATO to absorb the costs of accepting
credit cards, estimated to be almost 200
million dollars.
>> The tax officer saying no, a different
set of rules apply to us.
>> Now, tenants, too, are facing a squeeze.
Macquarie Bank's deft payment system,
which processes more than a million rent
payments a month, has also blocked
credit card payments.

never run a business, and they don't
understand what you need in that
flexibility of and how slim your margins
are.
>> Both the Prime Minister and Treasurer
are overseas, meaning if there is to be
an intervention, it won't come quickly.
Cameron Redden, News 24, Canberra.
>> And the small business ombudsman is
challenging the Australian Taxation
Office over its move to ban credit card
payments. The ATO has announced the
decision will come into effect from the
1st of December and the move introduced
after the government's ban on credit
card surcharges threatens to strip
businesses from the cash flow line. The
agency insists taxpayers should not be
footing the bill for merchant fees.

segments.text: When it comes to paying for things with plastic,
merchants need to know the rules to stay out of trouble,
and customers need to know the rules to avoid being ripped off.
Recently,
a Three news viewer emailed in asking what's OK
when it comes to credit versus debit cards.
So let's break that down.
Legally speaking,
in certain situations it is OK to charge customers for using both.
But there is some nuance to that.
There's a difference between a surcharge and a
convenience fee when it comes to processing payments.
A surcharge fee is a percentage-based fee charged on credit card transactions.
It's meant to cover the expense of a business accepting credit cards,
and credit card networks like Visa and Mastercard set limits on these fees,
capping.
Them at 3 or 4% of the sale.
Those card company limits are rules that businesses agree to
in order to be able to take those cards,
but they're not the law.
Federal law makes surcharge fees illegal on debit card transactions.
That's even if the debit card payment is being processed like
a credit card transaction without requiring you to enter your PIN.
But under Ohio state law,
convenience fees are legal on transactions.
That's regardless of the type of card you're using if you are using a card.
A convenience fee is a type of a percentage or flat fee
added on to your sale for a non-standard type of payment.
For example,
your utility company might charge a convenience fee for
allowing you to pay online or over the phone
when they typically accept payment by mail or in person.
This means that in most cases in Ohio you cannot be charged
a fee for using your debit card in person at a business,
but there's an exception for state entities under Ohio law,
so places like the BMV can charge a
fee for accepting payments using financial transaction devices
which are used to take credit and debit cards.
This is Stephanie Haney legally speaking for Three News.

Welcome to our deep dive on integrated payments and the potential benefits of becoming a wholesale ISO (Independent Sales Organization) for software companies. In a dynamic landscape where payment processing evolves rapidly, we help you navigate the key aspects to streamline your revenue streams and stay ahead of the curve.

In this video, we take an extensive look at what a wholesale ISO entails, its pros and cons, the registration process, responsibilities, costs, and crucial factors to consider before making this significant business decision.

A wholesale ISO is a unique opportunity for software companies to have more control over their clients' payment processing, pricing, and support. By embedding payment processing capabilities within their software and offering it as an additional service, companies can augment their revenues and improve their market positioning.

Throughout the video, we break down the benefits, including increased revenue, customized pricing, enhanced branding, and comprehensive support. However, we also tackle the potential challenges, such as heightened responsibility, high upfront and ongoing costs, and the complexity of managing a merchant portfolio.

Understanding the wholesale ISO registration process is crucial, which is why we guide you through each step from choosing a payment processor to the development of a payment processing solution. We also cover the main responsibilities and costs associated with becoming a wholesale ISO.

Lastly, we discuss when it makes sense economically for a software company to consider becoming a wholesale ISO. Factors such as the size of your client base, your ability to attract new clients, and how well you can manage the additional responsibilities are all examined.

Deciding whether to become a wholesale ISO requires a thorough understanding of the landscape and making informed decisions. This video will provide you with the knowledge you need to evaluate the potential return on investment and assess your readiness for the added responsibilities.

Watch now and unlock new avenues for your software business with wholesale ISO registration!
