And that is only the beginning. Because
now you need something even more
important than the machine itself, cash.
Lots and lots of cash. This is called
vault cash, and it is the money
physically loaded inside the machine so
customers can withdraw it. Most machines
need anywhere from $2,000 to $10,000
sitting inside them at all times,
depending on location traffic. Where
does that cash come from? Some owners
use their own savings. Others use a cash
vaulting service that loads the machine
for a fee, but takes a cut of the
profits in return. Either way, that
money is now sitting inside a metal box
exposed to risk waiting to be withdrawn
by strangers. And that leads us straight
into the next hidden cost that almost
nobody talks about, refilling the
machine. Cash does not last forever
inside an ATM. In busy locations,
machines can run dry within a day or
two. Someone has to physically drive to
that location, unlock the machine, and
reload it with fresh bills. That means
fuel costs, time, and sometimes hiring a
cash logistics company that charges per
visit. Now imagine owning 10 machines
scattered across the city. Suddenly this
passive income business is starting to
look a lot less passive. But we are
still not done with the costs. There is
also the location fee, sometimes called
a placement commission. Store owners do
not like you place a machine inside
their business out of kindness. They
want to cut, too. Usually a percentage
of the surcharge fee or a flat monthly
payment for allowing the machine on
their property. Some high traffic
locations demand aggressive commission
splits, sometimes as high as 50% of your
surcharge revenue. Read that again. 50%.
That means in some deals, half of every
single transaction fee goes straight
into the store owner's pocket before you
even see it. Now let's add processing
fees. Every transaction runs through a
payment network, and that network
charges a small fee for handling the
connection. Then there is the wireless
or internet connection fee because most
modern ATMs communicate over a cellular
data plan to process transactions
securely, which is another $20 to $40 a
month per machine. Then comes insurance
because if that machine gets damaged,
robbed, or vandalized, you need coverage
to protect your investment. And finally,
maintenance. Machines jam. Cash gets
stuck. Screens break. Card readers
malfunction. Every one of these problems
costs money to fix, and every hour the
machine is down is an hour it is not
making you a single cent. So is this
business actually profitable? Yes, but
only if you do it correctly, and most
people do not. Let's run some real
numbers so you can see exactly what a
well-placed machine can earn. Imagine a
machine placed in a busy convenience
store doing around 150 transactions per
month at a surcharge fee of $3 per
transaction that generates $450
in gross monthly revenue. Add
interchange fees of roughly $0.50 per
transaction, another $75,
and gross revenue lands around $525
per month. Now, subtract a moderate 30%
location commission, about $157,
plus wireless fees, maintenance
reserves, and cash logistics, maybe
another $80. You are left with roughly
$280 to $300 in net monthly profit from
a single machine. That might not sound
life-changing on its own, but remember,
this is one machine. Now, imagine owning
10 of these machines spread across
different locations. Suddenly, you are
looking at potentially $3,000 a month in
net profit. That is when this business
starts to look genuinely powerful.
Location is everything, and I mean
everything. A machine placed in a dead
corner of an empty strip mall might
process five transactions a month. At
that volume, you will never even recover
your monthly wireless bill, let alone
your original investment. But a machine
placed inside a busy nightclub, a
casino, a music festival, or a
cash-heavy small business can process
hundreds of transactions in a single
week. The exact same machine. The exact
same fee structure. Completely different
outcomes. They get sold a machine by a
company promising passive income. Place
it in a convenient location instead of a
profitable one, and then wonder why they
are losing money every month.
So, now let's talk about something even
more dangerous, The scams hiding inside
this industry. Because this business has
become a magnet for shady investment
schemes. You've probably seen the ads.
Buy an ATM, place it, and earn passive
income for life. Here is the trap. Some
companies sell overpriced machines,
promise to help you find locations, and
then either place your machine somewhere
with almost zero foot traffic, or worse,
do not place it at all. You paid
thousands of dollars, and your machine
is sitting in a warehouse collecting
dust. Others operate what looks
suspiciously like a pyramid structure,
where the real money is made by selling
machines to new investors, not by
operating the machines themselves. If a
company is more excited about recruiting
you than showing you real transaction
data, that is a massive red flag. Always
demand to see actual transaction history
before investing a single dollar. Now,
let's talk about something that
terrifies every serious ATM investor.
Fraud and theft. Because remember, there
is real cash sitting inside these
machines. Criminals know this, and some
of them get creative. There is a
technique called skimming, where a small
device is secretly attached to the card
reader to steal card information from
unsuspecting customers. If your machine
gets compromised, you could face
liability issues, reputation damage, and
even legal consequences. Then there is
the blunt, physical version of the
crime. Machines get ripped straight out
of walls, dragged away with chains
attached to trucks, or blown open with
explosives in extreme cases. Yes, that
actually happens more often than you
would think. This means location safety
is not just about foot traffic. It is
about physical security, too. A machine
in a well-lit, monitored, high-traffic
area is dramatically safer than one
sitting alone in a dark parking lot at
3:00 a.m. There is a bigger threat
looming over this entire industry,
though, and it has nothing to do with
theft or scams. It is the slow, steady
decline of cash itself. Digital
payments, tap-to-pay cards, and mobile
wallets are eating into cash usage every
single year. Some countries have already
seen dramatic drops in cash withdrawals
as consumers shift toward digital
transactions. So, is the ATM business a
dying industry? A ticking time bomb that
current owners just haven't noticed yet?
Here's the surprising truth that even
industry experts debate constantly. Cash
usage is declining in certain
demographics, but it is not
disappearing, especially not in specific
environments. Nightlife venues, casinos,
cash-based small businesses, flea
markets, and festivals still rely
heavily on cash. Older generations and
unbanked or underbanked individuals
still depend on cash daily. And in some
lower-income communities, ATM usage
remains extremely strong. This means
smart ATM investors are not spreading
machines everywhere randomly. They are
hyper-focused on placing machines where
cash remains king, avoiding locations
trending toward fully digital payments.
This single strategic decision is often
the difference between a thriving ATM
business and a slowly dying one. Now,
let's dig into something most people
never consider, the tax and business
structure side of owning ATMs. Because
this is not simply buy a machine,
collect cash, done. Serious operators
typically register a formal business
entity, separate their personal finances
from machine income, and track every
transaction meticulously for tax
purposes. Depreciation on the machine
itself can actually work in your favor,
allowing you to write off part of the
equipment cost over several years. But
mismanaging this side of the business,
mixing personal and business funds,
ignoring bookkeeping, skipping tax
filings, can create serious legal and
financial headaches down the road. This
is a real business, not a magical
passive income lottery ticket, and it
needs to be treated that way. Now, let's
talk about scaling, because this is
where the real money starts to appear. A
single machine earning $300 a month is
nice, but it is not going to replace
anyone's full-time income. The operators
who actually build wealth in this
industry are the ones who scale
aggressively and strategically. They
negotiate better placement deals as they
grow. They build relationships with cash
logistics companies to reduce per visit
costs. They use route optimization to
service multiple machines efficiently in
a single trip. Some experienced
operators manage portfolios of 50, 100,
or even hundreds of machines across an
entire region. At that scale, this stops
looking like a side hustle and starts
looking like a legitimate, highly
profitable enterprise. But scaling comes
with its own dangerous trap. More
machines mean more cash exposure, more
maintenance headaches, and more
operational complexity. One poorly
managed location can quietly bleed
profits from an otherwise successful
portfolio if you are not paying close
attention. So, here is the critical
question every potential investor needs
to ask themselves honestly. Do you have
the time, the capital, and the
operational discipline required to
manage this business properly? Now,
let's address something that often gets
buried in these conversations, leasing
versus buying. Some companies offer
leasing programs where you do not own
the machine outright, but instead pay a
monthly fee for the right to operate it
and collect a share of the fees. This
lowers your upfront barrier to entry,
sometimes to just a few hundred dollars,
but it also means sharing your profits
with the leasing company indefinitely.
There is no universally correct answer
here. It depends on your available
capital, your risk tolerance, and how
confident you are in a location's
transaction volume. New investors with
limited cash sometimes lease to test the
waters, while experienced operators
prefer buying outright once they've
proven a location's profitability. Now,
let's talk about something almost nobody
mentions, negotiating your placement
agreement. Most beginners simply accept
whatever commission split a business
owner proposes. But experienced
operators negotiate aggressively,
starting with a lower offer and only
increasing it if foot traffic data
justifies a higher split. They also
negotiate exclusivity clauses so
competitors cannot place a second
machine and split the volume. Here's a
critical warning sign that should make
you pause before signing. If a location
owner insists on an unusually high
commission above 50% without strong data
to justify it, walk away. The math
simply will not work in your favor
long-term. Let's shift gears and talk
about something surprisingly important,
machine reliability and brand selection.
Not all ATM machines are created equal.
Cheaper, lower quality machines tend to
jam more frequently, break down faster,
and require more expensive repairs over
their lifespan. Established, reputable
manufacturers may cost more upfront, but
they often save money in the long run
through fewer breakdowns and longer
operational lifespans. This is a classic
case of paying more now to avoid paying
significantly more later in repair costs
and lost transaction revenue during
downtime. Now, let's talk about
something that could reshape this entire
industry in the coming years,
cryptocurrency ATMs. Yes, this is a real
and rapidly growing subcategory within
the broader ATM industry. These machines
allow users to buy or sell
cryptocurrency using cash, often
charging significantly higher fees,
sometimes upward of 10 to 20% per
transaction, attracting a new wave of
investors chasing higher margins. But
this segment carries unique risks,
including regulatory uncertainty, price
volatility, and increased scrutiny from
financial authorities. Some governments
have already introduced strict
regulations or outright bans on crypto
ATMs. This is a high-risk, potentially
high-reward niche, and it is not for the
faint of heart. So, is owning ATM
machines actually a good investment in
today's economic environment? The
honest, unfiltered answer is this, it
depends entirely on execution. This is
not a guaranteed passive income machine
that prints money while you sleep,
despite what slick marketing campaign
pains want you to believe. It is a
legitimate small business that requires
research, strategic location selection,
ongoing management, and a genuine
understanding of cash flow economics.
Done correctly, with well-researched
locations, fair commission agreements,
and disciplined operations, it can
generate meaningful, scalable income for
years. Done carelessly, chasing flashy
advertisements and skipping due
diligence, it can quietly drain your
savings while you wonder where all your
money disappeared to. If you are
seriously considering entering this
industry, do not buy a single machine
until you have personally verified real
transaction data from an existing
location. Do not trust promises. Trust
numbers. Visit potential locations in
person. Count foot traffic yourself. Ask
nearby business owners about existing
ATM performance in the area. Because in
this business, the difference between
wealth and financial disaster often
comes down to a single decision, where
exactly you place that machine. The
metal box sitting in the corner of that
gas station is not magic. It is simple
economics hidden in plain sight waiting
for someone patient enough to actually
understand how it works. Before we wrap
up, let's talk about a question that
comes up constantly in the comments. How
does the ATM business actually compare
to other so-called passive income
investments like rental real estate,
vending machines, laundromats, or car
washes? Here's an honest comparison
because I am not here to sell you a
dream. Rental real estate requires a
much larger upfront investment, but it
also tends to appreciate in value,
something an ATM machine will never do.
A machine depreciates and eventually
becomes outdated technology that needs
replacing. Vending machines share a
similar model to ATMs, low upfront cost,
location-dependent success, ongoing
restocking, but they sell physical
products with real margins, while ATMs
simply move existing cash and collect a
fee. Laundromats and car washes require
far larger capital and a physical
storefront, but can generate higher
monthly revenue once established. So,
where does the ATM business fit? An
interesting middle ground. Lower barrier
to entry than real estate, but genuinely
scalable if you master location
selection. Industry insiders call it a
boring but steady business, capable of
producing consistent monthly cash flow
when managed correctly. Now, let's
address something that catches almost
every beginner off guard, seasonality.
Many people assume ATM income stays the
same every month, but that is rarely
true. Machines near tourist attractions
or festivals can see massive spikes
during peak season, followed by a
dramatic drop in the off-season.
Machines near college campuses see
predictable dips during summer and
winter break. Some experienced owners
even relocate machines temporarily,
moving a unit from a slow winter
location to a booming summer festival
circuit. That flexibility separates
casual hobbyists from serious operators
treating this as a genuine business.
Now, let's talk briefly about something
rarely discussed, but incredibly
important, exit strategy. What happens
when you eventually want to sell your
ATM business or a portion of your
machine portfolio? Unlike real estate,
there is no massive liquid marketplace
constantly buying and selling used ATM
machines and their placement contracts.
However, a proven profitable route with
strong transaction history can
absolutely be sold to another operator,
sometimes for a premium above the value
of the physical machines themselves.
Buyers are essentially purchasing the
income stream and the relationship with
the location, not just the metal box
sitting on the floor. This means
documentation matters immensely. Keeping
clean, organized transaction records
from day one significantly increases the
resale value of your route down the
line. Operators who neglect this
paperwork often struggle to prove their
business is legitimate when it comes
time to sell. So, here is a quick recap
of everything we covered because this
was a lot of information. ATM machines
earn money through two channels,
surcharge fees paid by the customer and
smaller interchange fees paid by the
customer's bank. Against that revenue
sits a long list of hidden costs. The
machine itself, vault cash, cash
logistics, location commissions,
wireless connectivity, insurance, and
ongoing maintenance. Location is the
single most important variable
determining whether a machine becomes a
profitable asset or a slowly draining
liability. The industry has its share of
predatory sellers and scams, so
verifying real transaction data before
investing is non-negotiable. Cash is
declining in some sectors of the
economy, but remains strong in specific
cash-heavy environments, meaning smart
placement matters more today than ever
before. And finally, this business
rewards operators who treat it
seriously, negotiate placement terms,
manage cash flow carefully, and think
strategically about scaling rather than
those chasing a fantasy of effortless
passive income. If you take one single
lesson away from everything we just
covered, let it be this. The machine is
never the business. The location is the
business. Anyone can buy a metal box
with a screen and a cash dispenser. Very
few people take the time to actually
understand where that box needs to sit,
who needs to walk past it, and why they
will reach for their card the moment
they see it. That single piece of
knowledge is worth more than every
machine, every lease deal, and every
flashy advertisement promising overnight
passive income combined. If this
breakdown opened your eyes to how this
hidden industry really operates, make
sure you are subscribed because there is
an entire world of businesses like this
one that most people never even think to
look into. And trust me, some of the
next ones are even more surprising than
this.

A machine in a well-lit, monitored, high-traffic area is dramatically safer than one sitting alone in a dark parking lot at 3:00 a.m. There is a bigger threat looming over this entire industry, though, and it has nothing to do with theft or scams. It is the slow, steady decline of cash itself. Digital payments, tap-to-pay cards, and mobile wallets are eating into cash usage every single year. Some countries have already seen dramatic drops in cash withdrawals as consumers shift toward digital transactions. So, is the ATM business a dying industry? A ticking time bomb that current owners just haven't noticed yet? Here's the surprising truth that even industry experts debate constantly. Cash usage is declining in certain demographics, but it is not disappearing, especially not in specific environments. Nightlife venues, casinos, cash-based small businesses, flea markets, and festivals still rely heavily on cash. Older generations and unbanked or underbanked individuals still depend on cash daily. And in some lower-income communities, ATM usage remains extremely strong. This means smart ATM investors are not spreading machines everywhere randomly. They are hyper-focused on placing machines where cash remains king, avoiding locations trending toward fully digital payments. This single strategic decision is often the difference between a thriving ATM business and a slowly dying one. Now, let's dig into something most people never consider, the tax and business structure side of owning ATMs. Because this is not simply buy a machine, collect cash, done. Serious operators typically register a formal business entity, separate their personal finances from machine income, and track every transaction meticulously for tax purposes. Depreciation on the machine itself can actually work in your favor, allowing you to write off part of the equipment cost over several years. But mismanaging this side of the business, mixing personal and business funds, ignoring bookkeeping, skipping tax filings, can create serious legal and financial headaches down the road. This is a real business, not a magical passive income lottery ticket, and it needs to be treated that way. Now, let's talk about scaling, because this is where the real money starts to appear. A single machine earning $300 a month is nice, but it is not going to replace anyone's full-time income. The operators who actually build wealth in this industry are the ones who scale aggressively and strategically. They negotiate better placement deals as they grow. They build relationships with cash logistics companies to reduce per visit costs. They use route optimization to service multiple machines efficiently in a single trip. Some experienced operators manage portfolios of 50, 100, or even hundreds of machines across an entire region. At that scale, this stops looking like a side hustle and starts looking like a legitimate, highly profitable enterprise. But scaling comes with its own dangerous trap. More machines mean more cash exposure, more maintenance headaches, and more operational complexity. One poorly managed location can quietly bleed profits from an otherwise successful portfolio if you are not paying close attention. So, here is the critical question every potential investor needs to ask themselves honestly. Do you have the time, the capital, and the operational discipline required to manage this business properly? Now, let's address something that often gets buried in these conversations, leasing versus buying. Some companies offer leasing programs where you do not own the machine outright, but instead pay a monthly fee for the right to operate it and collect a share of the fees. This lowers your upfront barrier to entry, sometimes to just a few hundred dollars, but it also means sharing your profits with the leasing company indefinitely. There is no universally correct answer here. It depends on your available capital, your risk tolerance, and how confident you are in a location's transaction volume. New investors with limited cash sometimes lease to test the waters, while experienced operators prefer buying outright once they've proven a location's profitability. Now, let's talk about something almost nobody mentions, negotiating your placement agreement. Most beginners simply accept whatever commission split a business owner proposes. But experienced operators negotiate aggressively, starting with a lower offer and only increasing it if foot traffic data justifies a higher split. They also negotiate exclusivity clauses so competitors cannot place a second machine and split the volume. Here's a critical warning sign that should make you pause before signing. If a location owner insists on an unusually high commission above 50% without strong data to justify it, walk away. The math simply will not work in your favor long-term. Let's shift gears and talk about something surprisingly important, machine reliability and brand selection. Not all ATM machines are created equal. Cheaper, lower quality machines tend to jam more frequently, break down faster, and require more expensive repairs over their lifespan. Established, reputable manufacturers may cost more upfront, but they often save money in the long run through fewer breakdowns and longer operational lifespans. This is a classic case of paying more now to avoid paying significantly more later in repair costs and lost transaction revenue during downtime. Now, let's talk about something that could reshape this entire industry in the coming years, cryptocurrency ATMs. Yes, this is a real and rapidly growing subcategory within the broader ATM industry. These machines allow users to buy or sell cryptocurrency using cash, often charging significantly higher fees, sometimes upward of 10 to 20% per transaction, attracting a new wave of investors chasing higher margins. But this segment carries unique risks, including regulatory uncertainty, price volatility, and increased scrutiny from financial authorities. Some governments have already introduced strict regulations or outright bans on crypto ATMs. This is a high-risk, potentially high-reward niche, and it is not for the faint of heart. So, is owning ATM machines actually a good investment in today's economic environment? The honest, unfiltered answer is this, it depends entirely on execution. This is not a guaranteed passive income machine that prints money while you sleep, despite what slick marketing campaign pains want you to believe. It is a legitimate small business that requires research, strategic location selection, ongoing management, and a genuine understanding of cash flow economics. Done correctly, with well-researched locations, fair commission agreements, and disciplined operations, it can generate meaningful, scalable income for years. Done carelessly, chasing flashy advertisements and skipping due diligence, it can quietly drain your savings while you wonder where all your money disappeared to. If you are seriously considering entering this industry, do not buy a single machine until you have personally verified real transaction data from an existing location. Do not trust promises. Trust numbers. Visit potential locations in person. Count foot traffic yourself. Ask nearby business owners about existing ATM performance in the area. Because in this business, the difference between wealth and financial disaster often comes down to a single decision, where exactly you place that machine. The metal box sitting in the corner of that gas station is not magic. It is simple economics hidden in plain sight waiting for someone patient enough to actually understand how it works. Before we wrap up, let's talk about a question that comes up constantly in the comments. How does the ATM business actually compare to other so-called passive income investments like rental real estate, vending machines, laundromats, or car washes? Here's an honest comparison because I am not here to sell you a dream. Rental real estate requires a much larger upfront investment, but it also tends to appreciate in value, something an ATM machine will never do. A machine depreciates and eventually becomes outdated technology that needs replacing. Vending machines share a similar model to ATMs, low upfront cost, location-dependent success, ongoing restocking, but they sell physical products with real margins, while ATMs simply move existing cash and collect a fee. Laundromats and car washes require far larger capital and a physical storefront, but can generate higher monthly revenue once established. So, where does the ATM business fit? An interesting middle ground. Lower barrier to entry than real estate, but genuinely scalable if you master location selection. Industry insiders call it a boring but steady business, capable of producing consistent monthly cash flow when managed correctly. Now, let's address something that catches almost every beginner off guard, seasonality. Many people assume ATM income stays the same every month, but that is rarely true. Machines near tourist attractions or festivals can see massive spikes during peak season, followed by a dramatic drop in the off-season. Machines near college campuses see predictable dips during summer and winter break. Some experienced owners even relocate machines temporarily, moving a unit from a slow winter location to a booming summer festival circuit. That flexibility separates casual hobbyists from serious operators treating this as a genuine business. Now, let's talk briefly about something rarely discussed, but incredibly important, exit strategy. What happens when you eventually want to sell your ATM business or a portion of your machine portfolio? Unlike real estate, there is no massive liquid marketplace constantly buying and selling used ATM machines and their placement contracts. However, a proven profitable route with strong transaction history can absolutely be sold to another operator, sometimes for a premium above the value of the physical machines themselves. Buyers are essentially purchasing the income stream and the relationship with the location, not just the metal box sitting on the floor. This means documentation matters immensely. Keeping clean, organized transaction records from day one significantly increases the resale value of your route down the line. Operators who neglect this paperwork often struggle to prove their business is legitimate when it comes time to sell. So, here is a quick recap of everything we covered because this was a lot of information. ATM machines earn money through two channels, surcharge fees paid by the customer and smaller interchange fees paid by the customer's bank. Against that revenue sits a long list of hidden costs. The machine itself, vault cash, cash logistics, location commissions, wireless connectivity, insurance, and ongoing maintenance. Location is the single most important variable determining whether a machine becomes a profitable asset or a slowly draining liability. The industry has its share of predatory sellers and scams, so verifying real transaction data before investing is non-negotiable. Cash is declining in some sectors of the economy, but remains strong in specific cash-heavy environments, meaning smart placement matters more today than ever before. And finally, this business rewards operators who treat it seriously, negotiate placement terms, manage cash flow carefully, and think strategically about scaling rather than those chasing a fantasy of effortless passive income. If you take one single lesson away from everything we just covered, let it be this. The machine is never the business. The location is the business. Anyone can buy a metal box with a screen and a cash dispenser. Very few people take the time to actually understand where that box needs to sit, who needs to walk past it, and why they will reach for their card the moment they see it. That single piece of knowledge is worth more than every machine, every lease deal, and every flashy advertisement promising overnight passive income combined. If this breakdown opened your eyes to how this hidden industry really operates, make sure you are subscribed because there is an entire world of businesses like this one that most people never even think to look into. And trust me, some of the next ones are even more surprising than this.

If you're trying to find a decent source of passive income but haven't found any of the side hustles we've discussed in our previous videos to be the right fit, then you might be interested in learning about what it takes to start your own ATM business. 

▬Contents of this video▬
00:00 - Intro
0:14 - Buying an ATM
1:03 - Getting Your Paperwork
1:37 - Choosing a Location
2:15 - The Banking Agreement
2:55 - Setting Surcharge Rates
3:26 - ATM Business Profits

To own and operate an ATM, you don't need any kind of special training, experience, or technical know-how. All you have to essentially do is formulate a business plan, buy a machine, complete the required paperwork, find a suitable location, figure out what you want your surcharges to be, and then just sit back and let your ATM make you money. It's as simple as that. 

Most ATM machines these days charge between $2 to 5 for customers to access their cash. Obviously, you'll want to stay competitive with other ATMs in the surrounding area. Location will also play a significant role in determining what you should charge for your ATM's service. While a $5 ATM fee at a casino might be reasonable, folks trying to get some cash at a convenience store on a Tuesday night might not be willing to pay that kind of money.

All said done, after deducting operation costs, the average ATM owner makes about $600 a month per machine. Once again, depending on location, traffic, and surcharges, this number can fluctuate quite a bit.

After you've successfully set up one ATM, you can move on to purchasing other units to maximize your profit.

metadata.title: Where to Buy an ATM Machine (Without Getting Scammed)
metadata.author: ATMDepot - Make Money with ATM Machines
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about starting an ATM business but not sure where to actually buy your first machine? You're not alone.

In this video, we’ll break down the best places to buy an ATM machine, what red flags to avoid, and how to choose between new or refurbished machines—so you don’t waste time or money.

✅ We cover trusted manufacturers like Hyosung, Genmega, and Triton,
✅ Explain the difference between buying from a processor vs online,
✅ Share the must-have features for compliance and connectivity,

metadata.title: I Analyzed the Real Math of Owning 10 ATMs in America (2026 Profit Breakdown)
metadata.author: Lines & Gains
metadata.shortDescription:
Social media gurus love claiming that buying 10 ATM machines is an effortless $15,000/month passive income glitch. Today on Lines & Gains, we put a real 10-machine American ATM route ($28,000 hardware + $30,000 in rotating $20 vault cash) through our paper-and-pencil math test to see what actually lands in your bank account after store-owner surcharge splits, 4G cellular modems, vault insurance, and bank compliance fees (OutlierKit).

⏱️ VIDEO CHAPTERS (TIMESTAMPS):
00:00 The "$3.50 Per Swipe" ATM Myth vs. The $30,000 Vault Cash Reality
01:19 Real Startup Capital: 10 New EMV ATMs ($28K) + Working Vault Cash ($30K)
02:48 How 10 Cash-Venue ATMs Generate $12,250/Month (3,500 Withdrawals)
03:48 Audience Poll + The Expense Chainsaw (Store-Owner Splits, 4G Modems & Insurance)
06:33 The True Bottom Line: $7,825/Month Net Profit ($93,900/Yr for 6 Hrs/Week)
07:04 How to Avoid the Big-Bank Account Freeze + The $6.00 Festival ATM Multiplier ($10,225/Mo)

📈 Subscribe to Lines & Gains for weekly paper-and-pencil breakdowns of real US businesses and hidden financial systems!

segments.text: Every single week on Tik Tok and
Instagram, a guy in a rented sports car
stands in front of an ATM machine,
slides open the bottom steel safe, loads
a brick of $20 bills into a plastic
cassette, and tells you that owning 10
ATMs is the easiest $15,000 a month
passive income glitch in America. The
pitch sounds like fourth-grade math.
Every time somebody withdraws cash at a
bar, a nail salon, or a barbershop, they
pay a $3.50 surcharge fee. You get your
full cash wired back to your bank
account the very next morning, and you
keep the $3.50 as pure profit. But what
those social media gurus never tell you
before selling you their course is that
$30,000 of your own cash has to sit
locked inside those metal boxes earning
0%interest. And the second you withdraw
bricks of $20 bills every Friday, big
banks flag your business account for
money laundering and shut you down
overnight. Today, we are putting the
American ATM route business through our
paper and pencil math test. We are going
to build a real 10-machine ATM route
from scratch, calculate every single
swipe across high-traffic cash
businesses, subtract every store owner
commission, wireless modem fee, and bank
compliance cost, and see what actually
lands in your pocket. And stay until
part three because I will show you how
to get an official ATM vault bank
account that never freezes your money.
Plus the weekend festival ATM trick that
charges $6 per swipe. Let's start on day
one with the real startup capital
required for 10 machines. You never buy
used 10-year-old ATMs off Craigslist
because outdated card readers lack EMV
chip encryption. Meaning if a fraudster
schemes a card on your machine, you are
personally liable for every stolen
dollar. Instead, professional operators
buy 10 brand-new Genmega or Hyosung
commercial ATMs with the chip readers,
digital toppers, and heavy floor bolts
for $2,400 each or $24,000 Add $400 per
machine for heavy freight shipping,
commercial steel bolt installation into
the concrete floor, and wireless 4G
cellular routers, and your hardware cost
is $28,000. Now comes the hidden capital
wall that shocks beginners, vault cash.
An ATM without $20 bills inside it is
just an expensive paperweight. To keep
10 busy machines from running dry over a
Friday to Sunday weekend rush, you need
an average of $3,000 in $20 bills
rotating inside each machine at all
times. That means you need $30,000 in
working vault cash on top of your
$28,000 in machines, bringing your true
day one capital requirement to $58,000.
Now, how much revenue do 10 well-placed
ATMs actually generate? If you place an
ATM inside quiet retail store where
everyone pays with Apple Pay, your
machine will only get two transactions a
day and starve. Profitable ATM operators
only target cash-dominant venues, busy
10-chair barber shops, tattoo parlors,
late-night dive bars, cash-only taco
shops, independent dispensaries, and
nail salons where customers tip in cash.
Across 10 strong cash-heavy locations, a
healthy ATM averages 350 surcharge
withdrawals per month, about 11 to 12
swipes a day. Multiply 350 transactions
per machine across 10 machines, and your
route processes 3,500 withdrawals a
month at an average surcharge fee of
$3.50 per withdrawal, your 10-machine
ATM route generates exactly $12,250 a
month in gross surcharge revenue.
Earning $12,250 a month in gross fees
from 10 metal boxes. Sounds incredible
on paper. Bi-weekly, the federal ACH
settlement network wires your vault cash
plus your surcharge fees straight into
your account. But, before we open the
expense ledger and slice into that
$12,250, pause for 2 seconds and drop
your guess in the comments below.
When you place your ATM inside a busy
bar, tattoo shop, or barber shop, how
much of your $3.50 surcharge fee do you
think the store owner demands just to
let your machine sit on their floor?
Drop a dollar amount in the comments
right now and let's see who knows the
street rate. Here's the reality. Store
owners know their foot traffic is
valuable. In a small barber shop doing
200 swipes a month, you might pay the
owner $0.50 per transaction. But, in a
busy nightclub, dispensary, or nail
salon doing 400 swipes a month, store
owners demand a $1 to $1.50 commission
on every single withdrawal. Across a
10-machine route averaging 3,500
transactions a month, your average
location commission split is $1 per
swipe. That means $3,500 a month
vanishes right off the top into the
store owner's pockets. Expense number
two is wireless 4G communications, ISO
processing, and receipt paper. You
should never connect an ATM to a store
owner's public Wi-Fi because it drops
out and fails PCI banking security.
Every machine needs its own encrypted 4G
cellular wireless modem box costing $12
a month per machine plus thermal receipt
paper rolls and minor keypad or bill
dispenser roller replacements. Across 10
machines, wireless data and parts cost
$225 a month. Expense number three is
commercial general liability, inland
marine vault cash insurance, and GPS
trackers. Why do you need specialized
insurance and hidden Apple AirTags or
cellular GPS trackers inside every
vault? Because criminals with pickup
trucks and tow chains occasionally smash
through storefront glass at 3:00 in the
morning to drag an ATM out of a
building. Ensuring your 10 machines,
your $30,000 in vault cash, and your LLC
costs $350 a month. Expense number four
is vehicle gas, armored security habits,
and compliance banking fees. Driving to
10 locations once a week to load cash
cassettes, clear jammed $20 bills
wrapped in rubber bands, and pay monthly
commercial vault account wire fees takes
another $350 a month. Let's look at our
paper bottom line. Start with $12,250 in
gross surcharge revenue. Subtract $3,500
for store owner splits, $225 for
wireless modems and paper,
$350 for vault insurance, and $350 for
gas and bank fees. Your true net profit
landing in your bank account is exactly
$7,825 a month, or $93,900 a year,
for roughly 6 hours of work every week.
Making $7,825 a month in net profit
working 6 hours a week means you recoup
your entire $28,000 machine hardware
cost in just 3.6 months.
And remember, the other $30,000 of your
startup capital is still sitting in your
hands as liquid $20 bills. So, why do
50%of beginner ATM operators quit in
their first 90 days? Because of the bank
account shutdown trap. If you walk into
Chase, Bank of America, or Wells Fargo
with a normal business checking account
and ask the teller for $15,000 in crisp
$20 bills every Thursday morning.
Their automated anti-money laundering
software will flag your account as a
high-risk money services business and
close your accounts without warning. To
survive and scale in 2026, you must
never use a retail checking account for
vault cash. Instead, before you buy your
first machine, you register as an
official ISO affiliate through your ATM
processor and open a dedicated ATM vault
cash account with an ATM-friendly
regional commercial bank or use armored
vault cash provisioning once you pass 15
machines. Now, how do smart operators
take a 10-machine route making $7,800 a
month and push it past $11,000 a month
without signing a single new store
lease? By keeping two portable wireless
Event ATMs on heavy-duty wheel dollies
in their garage. Think about what
happens between April and October in
every American town. County fairs, food
truck festivals, beer gardens, rodeo
grounds, and outdoor flea markets where
vendors only accept cash or charge extra
for cards. Festival-goers happily pay a
$5 to $6 surcharge fee per withdrawal.
And a single portable ATM at a busy
3-day weekend festival can process 400
transactions in 72 hours
generating over $2,000 in surcharge fees
in a single weekend. If you want to
build a profitable ATM route without
getting burned, follow these three
ironclad rules. Rule one, open an
ATM-approved commercial bank account and
sign your first three location contracts
before you order a single machine. Rule
two, never load brand new sequential $20
bills that stick together or limp.
Taped-up bills that jam your dispenser.
Always use circulated fan banknotes.
Rule three,
put a 5-year digital location contract
in writing with every store owner so a
competitor cannot offer them 25 cents
more and steal your spot. Subscribe to
Lines and Gains for weekly paper and
pencil breakdowns of real US businesses
and click the video on your screen to
see the real math of owning a
self-storage facility.

segments.text: How to start a transaction online and finish it on a physical terminal?
The first step is to go to Device Management. Once
your merchant device is set up, click on the EPI and select Edit Parameters.
Next, navigate to the Terminal & Transaction section,
and then to the Valor Connect subcategory.
In the Cloud section, you can: Enable amount confirmation for handoff transactions, Set a
Valor Connect countdown to limit how long the transaction is active on the terminal,
which reduces exposure. And, on Android terminals,
enable menu options so the connection isn't lost mid-sale.
You can also: Display the terminal's default screen with the IP address,
Require the invoice number to be entered in the virtual terminal
before handoff. And activate enhanced retry logic in case of a failed attempt.
Once all settings are configured, download the parameter changes to
the device. These changes will reflect in the merchant’s virtual terminal.
After logging into the virtual terminal, you’ll see a Valor Connect checkbox in the
top right. Selecting it opens a dropdown that lists available devices—these could
be in different locations or used by different delivery drivers.
Below that, you’ll see a device connected to Valor Connect, ready for a transaction.
Let’s go ahead and select this EPI.
Now, add a line item to the transaction and apply any modifiers. Enter the required phone number,
and we’re ready to hand off the transaction to the terminal.
When we hit Process Payment, you’ll see the product details,
totals, and a prompt to proceed appear on the terminal screen.
On the terminal, tap Proceed, confirm Yes,

Once your merchant device is set up, click on the EPI and select Edit Parameters. Next, navigate to the Terminal & Transaction section, and then to the Valor Connect subcategory. In the Cloud section, you can: Enable amount confirmation for handoff transactions, Set a Valor Connect countdown to limit how long the transaction is active on the terminal, which reduces exposure. And, on Android terminals, enable menu options so the connection isn't lost mid-sale. You can also: Display the terminal's default screen with the IP address, Require the invoice number to be entered in the virtual terminal before handoff. And activate enhanced retry logic in case of a failed attempt. Once all settings are configured, download the parameter changes to the device. Merchant account pricing is often an apples to oranges comparison. 
So we’re gonna talk about interchange rates and pricing, Tier based pricing, flat rates, and how these compare to one another. 
So if you’ve ever wondered which rate structure is best, stick around because we’ll get into it here and at the end of the video I’ll give you the end-all be-all SINGLE comparison factor that you can use to compare ANY two merchant services providers to each other based on rates and price. 

ROLL INTRO

So rates and price… Everyone wants to know and thus, it’s one of the most common questions I get asked. 

And you’re probably considering your options and wondering for example… : “Why does Square have a fixed rate, but then all the merchant account companies have this thing called interchange plus?

Again I admit that it can be confusing to compare them. 

So to start, let me remind you about interchange... 
Interchange is a small fee paid by a merchant's bank (acquirer) to a cardholder's bank (issuer) to compensate the issuer for the value and benefits that merchants receive when they accept electronic payments. It enables banks that issue electronic payments to deliver tremendous value to merchants, governments and consumers.

So that’s the official definition...but in short, You can think of it as a base cost for all credit and debit card transactions.

A single interchange rate plus a transaction fee in most cases, is paid every time a transaction takes place and that goes for all 4 major card brands here:  Visa, Mastercard, Discover and AMEX. 
So, with that in mind let’s look at the first pricing model: 

Interchange Plus

This is also known as “cost plus” pricing model, and is commonplace in the merchant account industry.   It’s often the go-to pricing model for processors to offer to business owners. 

Here’s how it works: 

The merchant account provider simply passes through the network cost, which is interchange, and then adds a processor specific markup to cover other costs associated with maintaining that merchant account, such as administration fees, software and technology license fees, customer service, fraud and other risk factors just to name a few. 

There are 2 main variables within interchange plus pricing and they are: 

The % margin above interchange along with the per item fee above interchange 

And both of these things are applied every time a transaction takes place.  
Since there’s 100’s of interchange categories each with potentially different rates and transaction fees, this pricing model ensures a fixed margin of cost to you, the business owner,   while giving the benefit of having the actual interchange costs passed through to their account. 
Interchange plus is often regarded by industry payment professionals, as the “true” and “Transparent” rate structure when it comes to merchant account pricing. More on that at the end of the video…

metadata.title: Merchant Account Pricing: Interchange Fees Explained
metadata.author: Merchant Maverick
metadata.shortDescription:
Is understanding interchange fees giving you a headache? 

Every single credit or debit card transaction involves several business entities, and they all want their cut in exchange for the services.

We’ll explain what interchange fees (also referred to as interchange reimbursement fees) are and how they work.

Still have a question on processing fees & costs? Drop it below!

segments.text: Today's Maverick Minute is about...
Interchange fees.
In most cases, they are the single largest expense that you'll have to pay when accepting a customer's credit or debit card.
Understanding what they are and how they work might be giving you a headache. So we'll explain that for you.
Meanwhile, if you have a question, drop it below and subscribe to our Channel!
And now let's answer those questions!
Every single credit or debit card transaction involves several business entities,
and they all want their cuts in exchange for their services.
Interchange fees are also referred to as
interchange reimbursement fees. They are initially collected by the Credit Card Association that sponsor your customers card.
They are paid to the issuing bank
Which is the financial institution that sponsor your customers credit card.
That's kinda sound the same, right?
This is where it can get tricky...
See, Discover and American Express
function as both the sponsoring credit card Association and the issuing bank. On the other hand, Visa and MasterCard
barely slap their logo on cards that are actually issued by a bank.
And since the issuing bank is the entity advancing credits to consumers and taking on that associated risk,
they end up collecting almost all the interchange fees charged per transaction.
Here's another fun fact! All four
credit card associations
publish their own interchange rate schedules that cover every possible type of transaction you could encounter.
And since Visa and MasterCard
don't serve as
issuing bank, they charge a separate Network fee per transaction,
which also comes out of your total processing costs.
They're pretty small though around 0.5% and aren't considered part of the interchange fee. But you should be aware of it.
What's important for you to understand
is that, while you'll have to pay the interchange on every single credit or debit card transaction,
it's only part of your total cost for processing. Because guess what? Your merchant services provider needs their cut, too!
All in all, the interchange is the single largest expense in processing a transaction.
And depending on your processing rate plan,
roughly 70% to 90% of the transaction processing costs go to paying the interchange fees.
The rest goes to your
processor and the credit card Association.
Interchange rates for credit cards are usually around 6 times higher than they are for Debit cards.
Reward cards will have a higher interchange fee. Also, remember what we mentioned earlier,
each credit card brand has their own fee schedule. Since credit card
processors still have to pay the interchange fee and still charge for their services,
they've come up with ways to pass those costs on to you.
Note that when discussing a processing rate plan,
they often refer to costs they pay as wholesale rate.
This is essentially the same as the interchanging fee.
Processing rate plans generally follow 1 of 2 approaches. Either through a “pass-through” method found in interchange-plus and
subscription pricing plans; or through a “blended strategy” found in flat-rate and tiered pricing plans.
For a full breakdown on these pricing structures
I recommend you to check out our website!
And now be careful if a sales representative from a merchant account service provider offers you a
discount on the standard published interchange rates. The only way for you to eliminate or reduce
the interchange cost is by passing them on to your customers, which is
a whole ‘nother can of worms.
But for now, you're done with the headaches!
And if you're ready to dive into numbers, go click the link below and see you next week!
Check our playlist for more credit card processing and small business tips!

Next in the transactional bucket are dues and assessments. They're typically based on the total transaction volume that you process on a monthly basis. And you can identify them on your statements by looking for words like merit one, e-commerce, CNP fees, NABU, APF, and data usage fees. Dues and assessments largely fall into that wholesale category I talked about and are generally non-negotiable. So honestly, you don't need to spend that much time on them. But the next time you look at your statement and you see merit 1 or NABU or CMP, just know it's a due or assessment. It's a wholesale fee. You really can't touch those. To sum up, the key takeaway for transactional fees is that the cost you pay varies based on the type of transaction you're running, the type of credit card you're running, and how much markup your processor is adding to those wholesale rates. Remember, all of those variable wholesale rates are determined by Visa and Mastercard and are linked in our description below. Even if you spend 10 or 15 minutes looking through those rates to understand which ones might apply to you, that'll be time well spent. So, now we understand the transactional fees. The next bucket is the flat fees bucket. Flat fees vary by name, value, and applicability, but at least some of them are going to show up on your credit card processing statements. And there are three major types of flat fees: standard, add-on service, and junk fees. Let's start with the standard fees. These are predictable fees, and they generally come up every month. The first standard flat fee is the monthly fee. Most credit card processors charge a monthly fee, but they all seem to call it something different. It might be called an admin fee, a statement fee, or a maintenance fee, but it all really just serves as your base monthly processing fee. The average cost of monthly fees is about 10 to 35 bucks a month, but the ideal cost should be about 8 to 20 a month. If you're paying more than 20 bucks a month, you can probably reach out and try to negotiate a lower monthly fee. The next standard monthly fee is the monthly minimum fee. It's basically a minimum fee the credit card processors want you to pay to protect themselves against the possibility of a dormant merchant account. There are costs associated with keeping an account active. And if you're not processing anything, your account is likely costing the processor money. With that said, a lot of good processors don't charge a monthly minimum. So, if you see something like that on your statement, which ranges from 20 to about 40 bucks, you can probably call your processor and get it negotiated down to zero. Next up is the IRS report fee. Some processors charge a small fee for filing your annual transaction volume with the IRS. I mean, it's understandable. It's a cost to them. It usually ranges from 20 to 35 bucks, but the ideal cost should be zero to 20 bucks, somewhere around there. Next up is the PCI compliance fee. This one's confusing for a lot of business owners. It's like, what is PCI compliance anyway? In a nutshell, PCI compliance is basically a way for them to get you to adhere to some fraud protection standards. We've written an article about this linked in the description below if you want to dive a little deeper into that. Great. Otherwise, just know that PCI compliance fees are generally standard, but shouldn't be charged, in my opinion. If you see this on your statement, it's generally from 80 to about 120 bucks. You can chat with your processor to find out why you're being charged the fee and how you can get into compliance so they don't charge you for it. Similarly, there's the PCI non-compliance fee. They're pretty much the same thing. So, if you see this on your statement, you really want to chat with your processor and find out why you're being charged and how you can get rid of it. Next up in the flat fee bucket are the add-on service fees. And the first one is a terminal purchase fee. You know the credit card terminal that you use. A lot of processors will want you to buy the terminal off of them and cost ranges from about 200 to 400 bucks. Some terminals are fancier than others, so they might be more or less expensive, but anywhere between 150 to 350 is probably something you're going to have to pay to buy a terminal. It's a reasonable cost and it's fine. Next up is a terminal lease fee. So, instead of buying the terminal outright, some credit card processors allow you to lease the terminal like you would lease a car, which is an absolutely horrible deal because it'll end up costing you thousands of dollars for a $200 to $300 piece of equipment. Don't ever get a terminal lease. Some processors will give you a free terminal, but they'll charge what's called a terminal insurance fee. Obviously, they're covering the cost of the terminals. They want to make sure you don't break it or lose it or whatever. So, they might charge you anywhere from 80 to 150 bucks, but in my opinion, you might as well just buy the whole thing outright. Next up are the payment gateway and virtual terminal monthly fees. Sometimes processors will give you one for free, but it generally costs 10 to 20 bucks a month. Some processors will also charge a payment gateway or virtual terminal setup fee, but in my opinion, they shouldn't be charging you that. And the average cost is about 15 to 25 bucks a month. Some processors charge a merchant club fee that includes some benefits like free printer paper or whatever other garbage, but most of the time it's not worth it. I think it's like 5 to 15 bucks a month, but you definitely don't need to be in a merchant club. And lastly, the terminal reprogramming fee. If you already have an existing terminal from another credit card processor and you move to a new place, they might charge you a reprogramming fee. It's a onetime fee, probably 100 bucks on average, you can probably negotiate that down to zero, too. metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I explain how Interchange Plus pricing helps growing businesses save money on credit card fees.
📘 FREE EBOOK. Understanding Payments Get the full guide on avoiding hidden fees and protecting your business. 👉 Download here: https://link.helcim.com/0vanqK8n
💸 FREE TOOL. Compare Your Rates See exactly how much you'd save by switching to Helcim. 👉 Try the calculator: https://link.helcim.com/3TyYStwU

If you have ever felt confused by your merchant statement, you are not alone. Most business owners don't know exactly where their fees are going. In this video, I break down interchange plus pricing—the model that offers the transparency and scalability that growing businesses deserve.

Using simple sketches, I explain how interchange plus rates are calculated, why "flat rate" processors like Stripe or Square might be overcharging you as you scale, and how you can lower your effective rate to under 1.5% just by growing your volume.

⏰ Video Chapters:

0:00 - Intro: The Confusion Around Pricing
0:58 - The Two Pillars: Transparency & Scalability
1:24 - The Pie Analogy: Cost vs. Markup
1:56 - Where Does the Fee Go? (Banks vs. Processor)
3:19 - Why Costs Fluctuate (Debit vs. Corporate Cards)
3:50 - The Problem with Flat Rate Pricing
4:34 - How Interchange Plus Works
5:30 - Free EBook: Understanding Payments
6:03 - Scalability & The Rule of Large Numbers
7:33 - Volume Discounts: Lowering Your Markup
8:22 - The Payoff: What's The End Result?
9:08 - Free Statement Comparison Tool

💬 Interchange Plus FAQ

▶️ What are the components of interchange plus pricing? 
Processing fees are made up of two parts: the "cost" of the transaction (which goes to banks and card networks) and the "markup" (which goes to the payment processor to cover operating costs and profit).

▶️ How does interchange plus pricing work? 
Unlike flat-rate models, interchange plus separates the cost from the markup. If the transaction cost goes down, your rate goes down, ensuring you only pay exactly what is needed for that specific transaction.

▶️ Who sets interchange rates? 
The cost portion of the fee is paid to the banks (Interchange fees) and the card networks (Assessment fees), such as Mastercard, Visa, and Amex.

▶️ What are the benefits of interchange plus pricing? 
The primary benefits are transparency, which allows you to see exactly where your fees are going, and scalability, which rewards you with lower effective rates as your business grows.

▶️ Is interchange plus cost-effective for high-volume businesses? 
Yes, because interchange plus providers often lower their markup as you hit certain processing milestones, meaning your fees decrease as your volume increases.

▶️ Which payment processors offer interchange plus? 
Helcim offers interchange plus pricing, whereas other major processors like Square, Stripe, and PayPal typically use a flat-rate pricing model.

▶️ How do I calculate interchange plus fees? 
You can estimate your savings using our statement comparison tool that takes your current volume and card mix (online vs. in-person) to calculate what you would pay under an interchange plus model.

It’s not, the cards aren’t inserted in the terminal.

Okay, which is the highest cost bucket.

All right, and make sure that based on what I just said, make sure the statement adds

metadata.title: What Is Tiered Pricing? Merchant Services Pricing Explained
metadata.author: Joe Wagner | Merchant Services & Passive Income
metadata.shortDescription:
What is tiered pricing in merchant services, and why can finding a merchant on tiered pricing represent a major opportunity for a payment processing sales agent?

In this Merchant Service University training, I break down how tiered credit card processing pricing works, why it lacks the transparency of Interchange Plus pricing, and what merchant services agents should look for when reviewing a processing statement.

Tiered pricing typically separates transactions into three categories:
Qualified
Mid-Qualified
Non-Qualified

The problem is that merchants generally aren't given a clear view into how individual transactions are being routed between those tiers or how much markup the processor is actually earning.

The pricing may appear simple, but that simplicity can come at the expense of transparency.
That's one reason I prefer Interchange Plus pricing when a merchant wants to remain on traditional processing. With Interchange Plus, the underlying interchange costs and the processor's markup can be separated, making it much easier to understand what the processor is actually earning.

For merchant sales agents, there's another important lesson here:
When you find a merchant still using tiered pricing, pay attention.

It can be an indication that the merchant hasn't had their processing costs properly reviewed in a long time. Don't automatically assume you can save them money—but it absolutely gives you a reason to dig deeper, review the statement, and determine whether a better pricing structure is available.

In this video, you'll learn how tiered pricing works, what qualified/mid-qualified/non-qualified transactions mean, why the processor's markup can be difficult to identify, how tiered pricing compares with Interchange Plus, and how sales agents can turn a pricing review into an educated conversation with a merchant.

Visit https://www.ccsalespro.com/tieredpricing
Tiered Pricing is a common, yet often confusing, type of statement. It involves encountering several different categories on a tiered statement.
A very common structure is the three-tiered pricing system, which includes:

Qualified: Transactions involving standard cards that are presented at a physical location and approved.
Mid-Qualified: Often related to the method of entry, such as when the card is not present.
Non-Qualified: Typically associated with the type of card used, where rewards cards usually fall into the non-qualified category.

The most frequently encountered tiered pricing type on statements is the two-tiered system, which categorizes transactions as either card present or card not present

Another variant is the six-tiered pricing system.  This adheres to the traditional qualified, mid-qualified, and non-qualified categories, but also applies these classifications to debit cards.

ISO Amp simplifies the process of analyzing tiered pricing structures by both determining and clarifying the rates for each tier (no matter how confusing the statements may appear!) Your agents will not only be able to identify the structure but also easily convert statements to their preferred pricing structure.

metadata.title: What is Interchange Plus Pricing?
metadata.author: MerchantAccounts.ca
metadata.shortDescription:
Interchange plus pricing is the most transparent and best pricing model to use for credit card processing.  It results in the greatest transparency and lowest rates, which is especially important for large and high volume merchants.

In this video David explains what Interchange Plus pricing is, how it works, and a way to actually get lower interchange plus pricing from your existing credit card processor.  

Source:  https://www.merchant-accounts.ca

metadata.title: Understanding Your Merchant Statement: Everything They Don’t Want You To Know
metadata.author: PaymentCloud

Today, we're talking about a topic that's important for any business owner accepting card payments – reading and analyzing your merchant statement. 

Although every merchant statement is different, we’re going to give you some useful tips to help you make sense of yours, focusing on key components commonly found in merchant statements across the board. 

So, what exactly is a merchant processing statement? Picture it as a detailed report of your business's card transactions. It’s a monthly statement provided by your payment processor that breaks down all transactions, fees, and other important financial information for your business. 

And why does this matter to you? Well, understanding your merchant statement can help you identify discrepancies like unusual charges, errors, track your sales trends, and ensure you’re not overpaying in fees. It's like a financial health check-up for your business, giving you a clear picture of where you stand. 

Stick around through the whole video for a more detailed breakdown of all the elements within your statement.

Most business owners don’t choose their payment processing model — it’s chosen for them.

And because of that, many merchants don’t realize how much their pricing structure impacts what they actually pay.

In this video, we break down the three most common pricing models:

• Interchange Plus  
• Tiered Pricing  

You’ll learn how each model works, when each one makes sense, and why the wrong structure can lead to higher costs.

Understanding your pricing model is one of the most important steps in controlling your payment processing fees.

• How merchant services residual income actually works

Most merchant services agents never calculate this.

Once you understand your numbers, everything becomes easier:

• You know your goal
• You know how many merchants you need

👉 Most agents I speak to are stuck cold calling, door knocking, relying on referrals, and selling on savings or “support”…

If you’re already in the industry and want to:

• Get more deals
• Improve your positioning
• Build a real inbound lead system

segments.text: Hi, my name is James Shepherd.
I want to talk to you today just briefly about a big mistake that you don’t want to make
when you are doing a buy out.
Many of you are maybe you don’t even realize buy outs are a thing that you can do.
In this industry, when you get residual income, you can hopefully if you are with a processor
that allows you to own your residuals, you can sell that residual back to the processor,
or to a third party that buys portfolios.
I’ve had the opportunity over the last month to work with four different reps.
They were all working on doing a buy out.
There is one common mistake that all of them were about to make before they talked to me
at least.
I want to make sure you understand.
When you are doing a buy out, you are going to get a multiple on your residual.
For instance, a real common buy out in the industry would be something like maybe a 20X
to just make the math easy.
Let’s say that you have residual of $2,000 and you do a buy out or somebody is going
to buy your $2,000 a month.
You are not going to get that $2,000 a month anymore, but you are going to get a 20X, which
means you are going to get $40,000.
They are going to write you a check for $40,000.
Then they are going to take your $2,000 a month and you are never going to see it again.
They are making their money long term because they are going to keep getting $2,000 a month
and then it is going to slowly decline and those accounts are slowly going to cancel
off.
That’s a pretty simple thing.
Where buy outs start to get complicated with things called earn outs, hold backs, whatever
they want to call it, attrition bonuses or retention bonuses or whatever it is.
So what will happen a lot of times, the processor will say, “Hey, we are going to give you
a 20X buy out, but we are going to give you 12X up front.
Then we are going to give you another 4X after a year, if your attrition is less than 10%
or whatever.
Then we are going to give you the remaining 4X another year later if your attrition is
whatever.
Here is what you have to understand about that.
Nine times out of ten, those long term earn outs or hold outs or hold backs or whatever
they are, they don’t pay out.
The processor will design them in such a way that it is very unlikely you are going to
hit that.
What you need to make sure is that your buy out does not contain what I call an all or
nothing earn out.
An all or nothing earn out means, if you don’t meet this level, then you get nothing.
That’s a really bad deal.
A good deal would be, if you are going to get an earn out, say the one I just described
to you a minute ago.
A 12X up front would be pretty low, but let’s say you got that.
They said we’ll do a 20X.
You get 12X up front, another 4X in six months, and 4X in six months again over a year.
The key thing is that you get that 4X on whatever the current residual is at that time.
It can’t be you get that 4X as long as your attrition is here.
You’ve got to make sure you are going to get paid something.
So don’t agree to one of these deals where you have an earn out unless it is a really,
really good deal.
You’ve got to look at your portfolio activity because a lot of times, the processor can
really play games with that and they can set you up to get nothing.
Whereas instead it does make sense to say, “Okay, I get it.
You want to pay 12X based on what it is now.
As an insurance policy, you want to pay the other 8X over the next year based on wherever
it is at that time.”
That makes a lot of sense because you know there is going to be some attrition.
They want to pay out a little bit less, but what doesn’t make sense is for you to say,
“I’m only going to get my 4X if there is less than X amount of attrition” or whatever.
That can be a little bit scary.
One other alteration, or variation of that that will work for you is this.
If you are still selling for that processor and you intend to continue selling for the
processor, many times they will have a deal where they will let you replace accounts to
get your multiple.
That is totally fine as long as you are going to keep selling.
Let me explain the way that works.
The way that works is let’s say you got that 12X up front.
Then in six months, like we are going to give you another 4X, but your attrition can’t
be more than 10%.
If it is at say 15%, you are going to have to give us enough residual to replace that
extra 5% first.
Then we are going to give you the 4X.
That’s okay.
That actually does make a lot of sense.
You just have to make sure the attrition they are talking about is legitimate and it makes
sense, and you not going to end up giving up all your residuals just to handle a little
4X bonus.
So it is very important that you understand how they are going to pay out long term because
a lot of times sales people do a buy out because they are like, “Oh, I’ve got to have a
buy out.
I got to get this money right now.”
Take an extra week to make sure you are getting the right deal, because if you don’t get
the right deal long term, it’s a big problem.
If you are not happy with your up front pay out, don’t do the buy out because the odds
of you getting all your long term money are pretty slim unless you’ve negotiated in
exactly the right way.
If you have any questions about doing a buy out, or you have a buy out you are working
on and you want to ask me some questions.
I’ve done quite a few buy outs myself.
I’ve helped a lot of reps do a buy out.
Just comment below this video, or on our blog, or wherever.
Reach out to me on Facebook or Snapchat, or Twitter, or wherever you want to reach out
to me at and I’ll be glad to help you out and answer any questions that you have.
My name is James Shepherd.
Thanks for watching and listening.

metadata.title: How I Went from Riding the Bus to $190,000,000 in Merchant Services!
metadata.author: Residual Income for Beginners
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you leaving thousands of dollars on the table by only selling credit card processing? 💸

In this exclusive masterclass, 20-year industry veteran John Sarabia breaks down exactly how he went from taking the bus to building a network of over 3,000 sales partners! If you want to scale your residual income in 2026, you need to understand how to read statements and offer massive value to business owners.

First, John does a LIVE breakdown of a real restaurant's processing statement. He shows you the exact formula to calculate their overall rate, how to spot hidden debit card profits, and how to pitch the Cash Discount and Dual Pricing programs to save them up to $360,000 over ten years!

Then, we introduce the ultimate revenue multiplier: The Business Cash Advance (BCA) Program. Learn how to offer short-term funding (from $50k to $1M+) to businesses that need capital to grow. John explains factor rates, underwriting guidelines, preferred industries, and how you can make massive upfront commissions on every funded deal!

🔥 Ready to take action and build your passive income empire? DM me the word "RESIDUAL" on Instagram to join our FREE Community called "Residual Income for Beginners" where you can learn more about building wealth and watch FREE weekly LIVES, or simply click the link right here: https://go.cashswipe.com/skool

If you got value from this training, make sure to LIKE, COMMENT, and SUBSCRIBE to "Residual Income For Beginners" for more masterclasses on cash flow and financial freedom! 📈💳

39:00 - Closing Thoughts and Next Steps

segments.text: The battle over the Durbin Amendment,
how it affects consumers and businesses.
In this video, we will discuss the
Durbin Amendment, a part of the
Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and
Consumer Protection Act. This amendment
has significant implications for debit
card users and how much they pay for
their cards. We will explore the
background of the amendment, its two
main components, and the arguments for
and against it. Additionally, we will
examine how the amendment has impacted
businesses and consumers. Background:
The Durbin Amendment was passed in 2010
as part of the Dodd-Frank Act, a
response to the 2008 global financial
crisis.
Its purpose was to make the financial
system safer and prevent a repeat of the
crisis. The amendment created the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to
ensure fair treatment of consumers by
financial companies. However, it also
introduced regulations that affected
debit card transactions. The interchange
fee: One aspect of the Durbin Amendment
is the regulation of interchange fees,
which are fees paid by merchants to the
issuing bank for each debit card
transaction. The fee is capped at 0.05%
of the total transaction plus a flat fee
of 21 cents and an additional penny for
fraud protection. This fee is known as
the interchange fee or swipe fee,
although it is more complex than a
simple swipe fee. Impact on banks: The
Durbin cap affected banks with assets of
$10 billion or more, which were the
banks that received taxpayer bailouts in
2008. Smaller banks were not subject to
the cap. This regulation aimed to reduce
fees for merchants and in turn
potentially lower prices for consumers.
Unaffiliated debit network routing: The
second part of the Durbin Amendment
requires card-issuing banks to use at
least two unaffiliated network sources
for debit card transactions. This
provision promotes competition among
networks, potentially reducing fees for
merchants and consumers. By offering
more routing options, merchants can
choose the most cost-effective path for
their transactions. Arguments for and
against the Durbin Amendment. Supporters
of the Durbin Amendment argue that it
prevents a monopoly in debit network
routing, lowers interchange costs for
businesses, and promotes transparency in
the US bank card acceptance market. They
claim that the amendment has saved
consumers money, created jobs, and
increased the availability of free
checking accounts. Opponents of the
amendment argue that the savings from
lower interchange fees have not been
passed on to consumers. They claim that
the amendment has led to higher costs
for consumer banking, the elimination of
debit card rewards and free checking
account programs, and an increase in
unbanked individuals. Additionally,
compliance costs for community banks and
credit unions have risen, and businesses
with low to average sale amounts have
seen their costs increase. The reality,
research conducted by George Mason
University revealed that small
businesses have not experienced a
reduction in interchange fees, and
consumers have seen minimal savings. The
real winners of the Durbin cap are large
retailers and their investors, while
lower-income families are the losers.
Large retailers can negotiate lower
merchant service charges, and their
market dominance reduces the incentive
to pass on savings to consumers. Small
businesses have not seen their merchant
discount rates decrease, limiting their
ability to offer savings to consumers.
Conclusion, the Durbin Amendment, a part
of the Dodd-Frank Act, aimed to regulate
interchange fees and promote competition
in debit network routing. However, the
reality is that small businesses have
not benefited from lower fees, and
consumers have seen limited savings. The
amendment has resulted in higher costs
for consumer banking,
the elimination of rewards programs, and
an increase in unbanked individuals.
Ultimately, the winners of the Durbin
cap are large retailers, while
lower-income families bear the cost.
Sources, cardfellow.com and a George
Mason University research paper. As
always, do not forget to to and
subscribe to our channel All Things
Money, to see more content like this.
